path.title: UI/UX Design Foundations
path.subtitle: Make interfaces people don't have to read twice
path.summary: Most product folks treat design like wallpaper; pick a colour, add a gradient, ship. Then they wonder why every onboarding screen needs a Loom explainer. This path teaches the small set of decisions that separate an interface people glance at and use, from one they squint at and abandon. Five lessons, two named moves each, one capstone where you redesign a real-world Indian SaaS flow that almost works.

lessons.title: Visual Hierarchy: How the Eye Travels
lessons.subtitle: The eye is a lazy heuristic engine; your job is to bait it on purpose

audioChapters.label: Mental model: the lazy heuristic engine

blocks.md:
Open any SaaS dashboard in India built between 2019 and 2024. Count the buttons that are competing to be 'the' button on the screen. The number is rarely zero, often three, sometimes seven.

The people who built these screens were not careless. They had taste, they had Material guidelines, they had a Figma library. What they did not have is a clear opinion about where the eye should land first, second, and not-at-all. This lesson is that opinion.

blocks.alt: A cartoon eye on a treadmill, scanning a screen full of buttons, picking the loudest one labelled 'PAY NOW' while ignoring six grey ones around it.
blocks.caption: The eye does not read; it scans. Whatever has the most contrast wins, regardless of where it sits.

blocks.title: Mental model: the eye is a lazy heuristic engine
blocks.md: The visual system burns calories. To save them, it picks shortcuts: scan for the brightest, the most isolated, the most differently-coloured patch on the screen, and start there. **You don't get to override this. You get to design with it.** A screen that fights the heuristic loses; a screen that bait-and-switches it wins.

blocks.caption: Watch the eye-track heat-map travel across two versions of the same screen — same content, different hierarchy.

hi-IN.title: IRCTC ka case
hi-IN.md: Bhai, IRCTC khol ke dekho. Tatkal book karna hai. Screen pe 47 cheezein hai — ad, banner, login, captcha, sponsored ads, train list, fare, refund link. Sab ek hi shade ka neela. Eye thak gayi, finger Tatkal button dhundh raha hai bottom right mein. Yeh hierarchy nahi, yeh democracy hai. Aur democracy interfaces mein nahi chalti.

en.title: Same point, no train booking
en.md: Open the IRCTC site at peak Tatkal hour. Forty-seven elements, all the same shade of blue, none of them visibly the answer. The eye gives up; the user does too. A screen where everything is equally important is a screen with no hierarchy at all.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · F-pattern vs Z-pattern — How the eye actually moves across a page.

blocks.md:
**Contrast** is the cheapest, fastest, most reliable way to set hierarchy. Not size. Not colour-as-decoration. Contrast: the difference between the element and its surroundings.

A dark navy button on a pale grey card jumps off the page even at 12px tall. A 24px headline rendered in #6B7280 on a #F3F4F6 background disappears. The size doesn't matter; the contrast ratio does.

A quick number to anchor: WCAG AA wants 4.5:1 for body text. A primary CTA usually wants 7:1 or more against its surroundings, because you want the eye to land there first. If your primary button passes contrast checks but doesn't *visibly* dominate the screen, your contrast ratio is fine; your hierarchy still failed.

blocks.caption: Same layout, two contrast strategies. The right-hand screen tells you what to do; the left-hand one asks you to figure it out.

blocks.title: How to bait the eye in four steps

steps.label: Step 1 — Pick one primary action per screen
steps.body: If you have two primary buttons, you have one primary button and one regret. Decide which is the answer to the screen's question.

steps.label: Step 2 — Mute everything else
steps.body: Drop secondary buttons to outline-only or text-only. Push body text to a 70% opacity grey. The job is to make the primary stand out by contrast, not by being louder.

steps.label: Step 3 — Maximise the contrast on the primary
steps.body: Filled, dark, branded. Aim for 7:1 contrast against its background. If the rest of the screen is muted, even a small button dominates.

steps.label: Step 4 — Squint test
steps.body: Blur your eyes or shrink the screen to 25%. The primary action should still be the first thing you can identify. If not, you have a contrast failure.

blocks.prompt: On a settings screen with twelve form fields and a 'Save changes' button, what is the cheapest fix to direct the eye?

choices.label: Make 'Save changes' the only filled, dark button on the screen
choices.explain: Removes competition. The button doesn't need to be bigger; it needs to be the only one that looks like an answer.

choices.label: Add a coloured shadow under 'Save changes'
choices.explain: Shadows add depth, not hierarchy. If everything has a shadow, the trick is gone.

choices.label: Rearrange the fields by importance
choices.explain: Worth doing later, but does not direct the eye to the action. The eye is still hunting.

choices.label: Add a tooltip explaining the button
choices.explain: Microcopy fixes confusion, not invisibility. A tooltip you have to hover to see does not solve a discovery problem.

hi-IN.title: Pune ka design studio
hi-IN.md:
Ek Pune-based design studio mein junior designer ne kaha 'sir, button bada karna hai, pop nahi ho raha.' Lead designer ne pucha — 'screen pe aur kitne dark elements hai?' Junior bola — 'sab dark hai sir.' Lead bola — 'toh button bade karne se nahi, baaki sab halka karne se pop hoga.'

Yeh do ghante ki conversation thi. Insight free hai.

en.title: Same insight, no studio
en.md: A junior designer wants to make the button 'pop' by making it bigger. The lead asks how many other dark elements are on the screen. Answer: all of them. The fix isn't a bigger button; it's a quieter everything-else.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · Size weight contrast — The three levers of hierarchy.

blocks.md:
After contrast comes **position**. The eye has priors — left-to-right reading, top-to-bottom flow, the F-pattern on text-heavy pages, the Z-pattern on landing pages. These priors are real but weaker than contrast. They tie-break.

The useful version: **for two elements at equal contrast, position decides which the eye lands on first.** Top-left wins over bottom-right; the upper third of the screen wins over the lower two-thirds; isolated elements win over clustered ones. None of this beats a dark button on a pale background, but all of it matters when contrast is constant.

A practical rule: the most important action on a screen should sit either in the top-right of the header, or at the bottom-right of a card or form. Both positions are conventional, both are reachable on mobile, both are the last thing the eye sees on a left-to-right scan.

blocks.alt: A diagram showing the F-pattern reading flow on a text-heavy screen, with the eye sweeping the top, then the second line, then dropping down the left edge.
blocks.caption: On text-heavy screens, the eye traces an F. Most of the right column is read in peripheral vision only; that is where you put the things you do not need them to read.

coach.name: Studio-Lead Saanvi
coach.role: design lead, 9 years across India and Singapore

intro: Hi, I'm Saanvi. I've been a design lead at three SaaS companies, two in Bengaluru and one in Singapore.
I'm going to show you four real-ish design choices. Tell me whether each one strengthens visual hierarchy, weakens it, or has no effect.
There's no trick scoring; the goal is to build the muscle of seeing hierarchy as a property of the whole screen, not a property of one element.

scenarios.situation: On a dashboard with five filled blue buttons of equal weight, you change four of them to outline-only and leave one filled.
scenarios.explain: Classic mute-everything-else move. The remaining filled button now wins by contrast.

scenarios.situation: You add a red border around your primary CTA so it 'really stands out'.
scenarios.explain: You now have two competing dark colours on the same element — the navy fill and the red outline. The eye reads it as warning, not as primary action.

scenarios.situation: You move the 'Save' button from the top-right of the form to the bottom-right of the form.
scenarios.explain: Both are conventional. Contrast is unchanged; position is still strong. This is a taste call, not a hierarchy call.

scenarios.situation: You bold every label in your form because 'labels are important'.
scenarios.explain: If everything is bold, nothing is bold. You have flattened the hierarchy, not strengthened it.

scenarios.situation: You add 32px of vertical space above the 'Submit application' button on a long form.
scenarios.explain: Isolation is hierarchy. White space around a button reads as 'this is the answer' even when contrast is identical to surrounding text.

scenarios.situation: You add a tooltip icon next to your primary CTA labelled 'Click here for more info.'
scenarios.explain: Adds visual noise next to the most important element. The eye now has to disambiguate two dots of attention. Tooltip belongs further away or not at all.

blocks.caption: Watch the trap happen live — and the fix at the end.

blocks.title: The classic trap: bigger is hierarchy
blocks.md: The instinct of every untrained designer is to make the thing they care about **bigger**. Bigger heading, bigger button, bigger badge. The result is two things competing on size, neither winning on contrast, and a screen that feels shouty and confused. **Hierarchy is a relative property of the whole screen, not an absolute property of one element.** Most hierarchy fixes happen by making other things smaller or quieter, not by making the hero thing louder.

blocks.prompt: Order the steps of a 5-minute hierarchy audit on an existing screen.

items.label: Squint test
items.detail: Blur your eyes; what is the first thing you see?

items.label: Identify the screen's intended primary action
items.detail: Ask three teammates; if you get three answers, the hierarchy is broken.

items.label: List every element competing for attention
items.detail: Buttons, badges, banners, anything saturated.

items.label: Mute everything that is not the primary
items.detail: Outline buttons, drop opacity on labels, kill decorative shadows.

items.label: Re-run the squint test
items.detail: If the primary still does not win, the contrast ratio is still wrong, not the position.

blocks.hint: Start with the squint test — it tells you whether you have a problem before you start solving.

blocks.instruction: You're designing the empty state of an invoicing dashboard. There are four things on screen: a heading 'No invoices yet', a paragraph explaining what invoices do, a screenshot of a sample invoice, and a button 'Create your first invoice'. Write 3-4 sentences specifying the contrast and position choices that would make 'Create your first invoice' the first thing the eye lands on.
blocks.expected: I would make the button the only filled, dark element on the screen — primary blue at 7:1 contrast against the off-white background — and place it directly below the heading with at least 32px of breathing room around it. The heading would be dark but smaller than the button's visual weight. The paragraph would be in a 70% opacity grey, and the screenshot would be muted further with reduced saturation, so it reads as supporting evidence rather than as a competing focal point. Squint test: only the button should be identifiable when the screen is blurred.

blocks.prompt: Which of these are hierarchy moves you can make WITHOUT changing the size of any element? (pick two)

choices.label: Increase contrast between the primary action and its surroundings
choices.explain: The cheapest hierarchy lever in your kit.

choices.label: Add 32px of white space around the primary action
choices.explain: Isolation is hierarchy. Same size, more weight.

choices.label: Bold every heading on the page
choices.explain: Bolding everything resets the hierarchy at a higher weight; the relative differences are still flat.

choices.label: Add a drop-shadow under the heading
choices.explain: Adds depth, not hierarchy. The eye does not go to whatever has a shadow; it goes to whatever differs from its surroundings.

hi-IN.title: Saas-bahu serial wala lesson
hi-IN.md: Ek Bengaluru SaaS ki founder ne saas-bahu serial dekha aur kaha — 'inka camera kya kamaal hai, jis pe focus karna hai usi pe focus rehta hai.' Sahi baat hai. Camera mein blur, lighting, framing — sab ek hi cheez ke liye: jis pe attention chahiye, woh pop kare. UI mein bhi same: ek primary CTA, baaki sab background score.

en.title: Same point, no serial
en.md: A Bengaluru SaaS founder once said the trick of soap-opera cinematography is that whatever they want you to look at is the only sharp, lit, framed thing in the shot. UI is the same. One sharp button. Everything else is set dressing.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The CTA That Was Wearing a Section Header
blocks.source: Anonymous senior designer at Khaata Cloud, a Pune-based SMB accounting SaaS
blocks.story:
Khaata Cloud's marketing landing page had been converting at **1.8%** for nine months. The growth team blamed ad creative. The PM blamed the price page. The CEO blamed *vibes*. A new designer joined in February and asked one question on her first Monday: *"Where is the CTA?"*

It turned out the CTA — a button labelled `Start free trial` — was styled at **18px, weight 500, charcoal-on-white**, sitting inside a section called "Get Started." The section header, also 18px charcoal, sat 24px above it. To a scanning eye, the button read as a *sub-heading* of the section, not a clickable thing. Eye-tracking from the analytics tool showed users looked at the area for **0.4 seconds** and moved on.

The fix was one Figma file and one Friday afternoon: button became **#1F6FEB at 16px weight 600 with 14px vertical padding**, the section header dropped to a 14px uppercase eyebrow, and the surrounding 11 paragraphs of marketing prose got nuked. No copy change. No new feature. No A/B test infrastructure either — they shipped to 100% on a Tuesday because the old number was so bad the risk was zero.

New conversion four weeks later: **4.7%**. The CEO took credit at the next all-hands.
blocks.takeaway: If your CTA looks like a heading, the eye treats it like one. Hierarchy is not decoration; it is instruction.

blocks.title: Vikram's Three Mockups
blocks.setup:
You are freelancing for **Saral Pay**, a Bengaluru-based consumer fintech. Their founder **Vikram** — ex-payments engineer, first-time design buyer — is about to ship his first major redesign over Q2-Q3 2026. He slacks you at 9:14am on a Tuesday: *"I made three versions of the new home screen in Figma. Can you tell me which CTA hierarchy is right? Demo to investors is Friday."*

You open the file. There are indeed three frames, and they are *all wrong in different ways*.

coach.name: Design-Director Diya
coach.role: Your old boss from your agency days, now on speed-dial for sanity checks

stages.prompt: **Mockup A** has three buttons of equal size and weight: `Send Money`, `Pay Bills`, `Invest`. All charcoal-on-white, all 16px, evenly spaced. Vikram says: *"It's fair — every product gets equal billing."* What do you tell him?

options.label: "Looks clean. Ship it — fairness is a good principle."
options.explain: Fairness is a *political* principle, not a design one. Three equal CTAs means the eye picks one at random, which means **most users pick none**. Vikram's investor demo will show three users hovering, no one clicking. Diya is grimacing.

options.label: "Pick the one CTA that drives 70% of revenue. Make it primary. Demote the other two to text links or secondary buttons."
options.explain: **Yes.** Hierarchy is a forcing function: it asks the business *what matters most on this screen?* Vikram thinks for a second and says *"Send Money — it's 80% of our volume."* Now you have one job, not three.

options.label: "Make all three buttons bigger and brighter so they pop more."
options.explain: If everything shouts, nothing is heard. Three primary buttons is the same problem as three equal buttons, just louder. The eye still can't choose.

options.label: "Add a hero illustration above to draw the eye, then keep the three equal buttons."
options.explain: You added a *fourth* visual element competing with the three equal ones. The eye now travels: illustration, button, button, button, exit. Decoration does not solve a hierarchy problem; it usually compounds it.

stages.prompt: **Mockup B** has `Send Money` as a giant **#0EA5E9 cyan** button taking up 60% of the screen width, with `Pay Bills` and `Invest` as tiny grey text links underneath. Vikram says: *"You said make the primary one big. I made it big."* Your move?

options.label: "Perfect. Ship it."
options.explain: Big is not the same as *appropriate*. A 60%-width hero button on a home screen feels like a landing-page CTA, not an app primary action. Users will tap it accidentally on the way to their balance. Vikram will spend Friday explaining accidental sends.

options.label: "Scale it back to about 40% width with comfortable padding. The hierarchy comes from contrast and weight, not size alone."
options.explain: **Right.** Three hierarchy levers — size, weight, colour — and you only need two of them firing for the eye to pick a winner. Cranking all three to 11 turns a primary action into an aggressive one.

options.label: "Keep the size but change the colour to brand-grey so it's less aggressive."
options.explain: Now it's a giant grey button — visually loud, semantically muted. The eye goes there but the brain goes *"is that even clickable?"* Worst of both worlds.

options.label: "Add a pulsing animation to the cyan button so users know it's the main action."
options.explain: If your hierarchy needs animation to communicate itself, the static design has already failed. Also: a pulsing cyan button on a fintech app reads as a phishing pop-up. Diya is on the verge of sending you a voice note.

stages.prompt: **Mockup C** has `Send Money` as a properly-sized cyan primary, `Pay Bills` as a secondary outline button next to it, and `Invest` as a quiet text link below. The balance card above is **48px bold**, the welcome message is **24px regular**. Vikram says: *"This one feels right but I can't say why."* What is your one-line answer?

options.label: "Because the eye has a path: balance, then primary action, then alternatives. Three stops, in order. That's hierarchy."
options.explain: **Exactly the move.** Naming the path makes Vikram a better client for the next 12 weeks. He now has vocabulary for *why* something works, not just *that* it does.

options.label: "Because the colours are nicer."
options.explain: Vikram leaves the meeting having learned nothing. Next week he'll ask you the same question about a different screen. You billed for an hour of insight and delivered a vibe.

options.label: "Because it follows the F-pattern that users scan."
options.explain: F-pattern is a finding from 2006 about long-form text on desktop. It does not describe a fintech home screen on a 6-inch phone. You sound smart and are wrong.

options.label: "Because it has more whitespace."
options.explain: Whitespace contributes, but it is the *consequence* of good hierarchy, not the cause. Vikram will respond by adding 80px of padding to every other screen and breaking the layout.

stages.prompt: Vikram says: *"Okay, Mockup C wins. But investors love a wow moment. Should we add a gradient or a glow on the primary button to make it feel premium?"* You have 30 seconds before he opens Figma to do it himself.

options.label: "No. The button is already the loudest thing on the screen by design. Adding a gradient is volume on top of a clear signal — it muddles, not amplifies."
options.explain: **Hold the line.** Hierarchy is the *system*; decoration is the *risk*. You just saved Vikram from a button that looks like a 2014 iOS skeumorph throwback.

options.label: "Sure, a subtle gradient is fine if it's on-brand."
options.explain: Vikram interprets *subtle* as *visible from across the room*. Friday's demo features a button that looks like the home screen of a 2007 BlackBerry. You are responsible for this.

options.label: "Add the glow but only on hover so it's a delight moment."
options.explain: Hover does not exist on mobile. The glow will never fire. You added complexity for a state 90% of users will never see, and the 10% who do will think it's a bug.

options.label: "Let's A/B test it."
options.explain: Vikram has 11,000 monthly users and an investor demo on Friday. You don't have the volume or the time. "A/B test it" is what designers say when they don't want to defend a position. Defend the position.

outcomes.perfect: Investor demo on Friday goes well. Vikram texts you Saturday: *"Two of them want to know who designed it."* You bill the hour, name the path, and protect the design from the gradient. **Diya is, briefly, proud.**
outcomes.good: You got Vikram to the right mockup but let one piece of decoration through. The demo lands fine but the cofounder spends ten minutes asking why the button glows. Re-read the lesson on hierarchy as system, not decoration.
outcomes.learn: Vikram shipped a home screen with three equal CTAs and a pulsing gradient button. The investor demo got *"interesting energy."* Re-read the lesson — especially the section on **size + weight + colour as a small set of levers**, not all three at once.

blocks.caption: Try (~60s) · Squint test — Toggle blur; see what survives.

points: The eye is a lazy heuristic engine. It scans for the loudest, most isolated patch first. Design with that, not against it.
Contrast outranks size. A small dark button on a pale screen beats a giant grey button every time.
One primary action per screen. Two primary buttons mean one primary button and one regret.
Position tie-breaks when contrast is constant. Top-right of the header or bottom-right of the card both win.
When a button doesn't 'pop', the answer is almost always to mute everything else, not to make the button louder.

blocks.prompt: Open one screen in any product you used today. Run the squint test: what is the first thing you can identify when the screen is blurred? Is it what the product wanted you to see? If not, where did the hierarchy go wrong — competing buttons, equal contrast, no isolation?

lessons.title: Layout and Grids — The Invisible Skeleton
lessons.subtitle: A grid is a contract; spacing is the punctuation

blocks.md:
Some screens feel calm. Other screens feel itchy. The itchy ones almost always have one thing in common: the spacing is wrong. Not the colours, not the type, not the copy. The padding around the buttons is 11px, then 14px, then 9px, depending on which engineer ate lunch first.

Layout is the discipline that makes a screen feel deliberate. The skill is not making things look pretty; it is committing to a small set of numbers and refusing to break them. By the end of this lesson you will have a spacing scale you can defend in a code review, and a grid that does the rest of the heavy lifting for you.

blocks.title: Mental model: the grid is a contract
blocks.md: A grid is not a visual aesthetic; it is **a contract you sign with your future self and your engineers**. It says: 'every spacing decision in this product comes from this list of numbers — 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64. No exceptions without a written reason.' The reason a system feels deliberate is that it has fewer choices, not more. The grid is what removes the choices.

blocks.caption: Toggle the 8-point grid overlay on a real screen and see which elements respect the contract and which freelance.

hi-IN.title: Mistry-bhai ka analogy
hi-IN.md:
Ghar banwa rahe ho. Mistry-bhai aaya, bola — 'sab dewar 9 inch ki, sab darwaza 7 feet ka, sab tile 2x2.' Tum ne pucha — 'aise kyun?' Bola — 'kyunki agar har dewar alag ho, electrician pagal ho jayega aur tum bhi.'

UI mein bhi same hai. 8-point grid yahi mistry-bhai wala discipline hai. Bina iske, har screen new construction project hai.

en.title: Same point, no construction
en.md: Imagine building a house where every wall is a slightly different thickness, every door a slightly different height. The plumber would lose his mind. Your engineers feel the same way when every screen has its own padding. The grid is the standard wall thickness.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · 8pt grid — Why 8 (not 7 or 9).

blocks.md:
Pick 8. Not because Apple did, not because Google did — because 8 has the cleanest factors of any small number that still gives you usable steps. Half of 8 is 4 (still on a pixel boundary). Quarter of 8 is 2 (still rendering crisply). And 8 multiplied gives you 16, 24, 32, 48, 64 — the entire spacing ladder you will ever need.

A defensible scale for a SaaS product:

- **4px** — the only sub-8 step. Use sparingly: tight icon-text pairs.
- **8px** — minimum gap inside a grouped element.
- **12px** — sub-step for tighter dense screens; use sparingly.
- **16px** — default padding inside cards and buttons.
- **24px** — gap between related groups.
- **32px** — gap between unrelated sections.
- **48px** — gap before a major page region.
- **64px** — page-level breathing room.

Notice what is missing: 11, 13, 18, 22, 30. They feel right by 1px to whoever drew them, and they are wrong by 1px to everyone else.

blocks.title: Adopting an 8-point grid in an existing codebase

steps.label: Step 1 — Audit current spacing
steps.body: Grep your CSS for px values. You will find dozens of unique numbers between 1 and 64. Most of them are within 2px of an 8-point step.

steps.label: Step 2 — Define the scale as tokens
steps.body: In Tailwind, this is mostly the default. Define spacing-1 through spacing-16 in your config, but keep the names usable: tight, snug, cozy, comfy, loose.

steps.label: Step 3 — Replace per-component overrides
steps.body: Sweep one screen at a time. The first three are slow; the next ten go fast because the patterns repeat.

steps.label: Step 4 — Add a lint rule
steps.body: Forbid arbitrary px values in className strings. The cost of slipping back is now visible in CI, not in code review.

steps.label: Step 5 — Document the exceptions
steps.body: Some places need a 6px badge gap. Fine — write down which and why, so the next person knows it was a decision, not an accident.

blocks.prompt: Why is 8 a better base unit than 10?

choices.label: Because 8 has clean half-steps (4) and quarter-steps (2) that stay on pixel boundaries
choices.explain: The divisibility is the whole reason. 10 gives you 5 and 2.5 — and 2.5px gets rounded inconsistently across browsers and density modes.

choices.label: Because designers prefer it aesthetically
choices.explain: It's not aesthetic; it's mathematical. Aesthetic preferences shift; the divisibility argument doesn't.

choices.label: Because 10 is too round and feels boring
choices.explain: Roundness has nothing to do with it. The argument is about sub-steps and pixel rendering.

choices.label: Because Tailwind uses 8 by default
choices.explain: Tailwind uses 4 as a base unit that composes into 8. Even Tailwind's reason is divisibility.

hi-IN.title: Bengaluru ka 200-person SaaS
hi-IN.md:
Bengaluru ke ek 200-person SaaS mein design lead ne ek Friday afternoon team ko bola — 'kal se sirf 8-point spacing.' Engineer bola — 'sir, abhi to bahut places hai jaha 11px, 13px, 22px hai.' Lead bola — 'haan, lekin ab tum agla 11px likhoge to PR mein roak laga doonga.'

Do months mein screen calmer ho gaye. Dev velocity bhi badhi — kyunki ab koi 'kitna padding' decide nahi kar raha, sab pre-decided hai.

en.title: Same point, no Friday standup
en.md: A 200-person SaaS in Bengaluru moved to an 8-point grid in a single sprint. The screens calmed down inside two months. Engineering velocity also went up — because nobody was negotiating the right padding any more, the answer was already in the config.

blocks.text: Move 2 — The gutter that earns its keep

blocks.md:
Once your spacing scale is locked, the next decision is the **gutter** — the gap between columns in a multi-column layout. The default gutter on a 12-column desktop grid is 24 or 32 pixels. The default for a single-column mobile layout is 16.

The useful version of this rule: **the gutter should always exceed the padding inside the columns**, otherwise your two cards look like one continuous strip with a vertical scratch through the middle. If your card has 16px internal padding, your gutter should be at least 24. If your card has 24px padding, your gutter should be at least 32.

A gutter that is too tight is a layout that feels glued. A gutter that is too wide is a layout that feels broken into islands. The Goldilocks zone for desktop SaaS is 24 to 32 pixels; for marketing pages where each section is a story, push it to 48 or 64. For mobile, you almost never go above 16.

coach.name: Studio-Lead Saanvi
coach.role: design lead, 9 years across India and Singapore

intro: Back to me. Today: spacing decisions, with no right answer in two of the six. Welcome to design.
Tell me whether each layout choice is sound, suspect, or actively wrong.

buckets.label: Suspect — defend it or fix it

scenarios.situation: Engineer adds padding-15 because the card 'looks better at 15px than at 16'.
scenarios.explain: Once anyone freelances by 1px, the contract is dead. The whole win of the grid is the discipline of the constraint.

scenarios.situation: Designer uses 12px padding inside dense data table cells.
scenarios.explain: 12 is on the scale (it's 8 + 4) and dense data-tables are the canonical use case for the sub-step. Defensible.

scenarios.situation: PM asks for a 'tight 6px gap' between two related metrics on a dashboard tile.
scenarios.explain: 6 is off-scale; you'd want either 4 or 8. Push back, suggest the nearest scale value, or write down 6 as a documented exception.

scenarios.situation: On mobile, you switch from a 24px gutter to a 16px gutter.
scenarios.explain: Standard responsive behaviour. Mobile screens are narrower so gutters proportionally shrink.

scenarios.situation: Card padding 24px, gutter between cards 16px.
scenarios.explain: Gutter narrower than padding makes cards feel glued. The gutter should always exceed the internal padding.

scenarios.situation: Marketing page uses 80px between major sections.
scenarios.explain: Off the standard scale (80 is 64 + 16) but defensible for marketing pages where each section is its own story; document it as an exception.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the 1px freelance
blocks.md: Every grid dies the same way. An engineer adds padding-15 because 'it looks slightly better than 16'. Three sprints later you have padding-13, padding-17, padding-22. None of them visibly wrong. Together: chaos. **The grid is a contract. The first off-scale value is the moment the contract dies.** Treat off-scale paddings the way you treat `console.log` in production: not catastrophic, but always a smell.

blocks.prompt: Order the steps for setting up a grid + spacing system on a new product.

items.label: Pick the base unit
items.detail: 8 unless you have a specific reason.

items.label: Define the spacing scale as named tokens
items.detail: spacing-1 (4) through spacing-16 (64) in your tailwind.config or CSS variables.

items.label: Pick a column count and gutter for each breakpoint
items.detail: 12-column with 24px gutter on desktop, 4-column with 16px gutter on mobile is a defensible default.

items.label: Apply to one screen end-to-end
items.detail: Pick the most-used screen; convert it fully before going wider.

items.label: Add a lint or design-token rule that forbids arbitrary values
items.detail: Make the next freelance painful. Tailwind's safelist or a custom ESLint rule both work.

blocks.hint: Start with the unit; everything else is derived from it.

blocks.instruction: You inherit a settings screen with this CSS: every input has padding 11px, every section has margin-bottom 17px, the page has padding 23px on the sides. Write a brief migration plan in 3-4 sentences: which scale you'd pick, which values you'd map the old ones to, and how you'd avoid silent regressions during the rollout.
blocks.expected: I'd adopt an 8-point scale and map the existing values upward to the nearest scale step: 11 becomes 12, 17 becomes 16, 23 becomes 24. I'd convert the spacing into named tokens (spacing-1 through spacing-16) in the design-token config so changes are global, not per-component. To avoid silent regressions, I'd ship the migration screen-by-screen with a visual diff in PR review, and add a lint rule that forbids arbitrary px values in className strings going forward. The first three screens will feel slow; after that the patterns repeat and the sweep accelerates.

blocks.prompt: Which two are signs your grid is being respected? (pick two)

choices.label: Designers and engineers can name the spacing scale from memory
choices.explain: Memorability is the test of whether the system has gone from policy to muscle memory.

choices.label: Most paddings in the codebase use named tokens, not raw px
choices.explain: Tokens decouple the value from the use, which lets you change the spacing scale without rewriting components.

choices.label: Every screen looks identical
choices.explain: The grid does not enforce uniformity of layout; it enforces uniformity of spacing values. Variety lives at the composition level.

choices.label: Engineers stop asking design about padding
choices.explain: If they stop asking it might mean the system works — or it might mean they're freelancing. The right test is whether the values they ship are on-scale.

hi-IN.title: Tata Sky ke remote ka design
hi-IN.md:
Tata Sky ka remote yaad hai? Buttons ka spacing perfect hota tha — chote chote thumb se bhi galat button nahi dabta tha. Wahin pe ek local cable wala remote dekho — buttons random spacing pe hai, kabhi 2 mil milimeter dur, kabhi sticking together. Aap mute karne ja rahe ho, channel change ho jaata hai.

Grid yeh hi cheez hai — physical product mein bhi, screen pe bhi. Spacing ka discipline hi accidents kam karta hai.

en.title: Same point, no remote
en.md: A premium TV remote has buttons spaced on a deliberate grid. A cheap remote has buttons that drift. Press 'mute' on the cheap one and you'll often hit 'channel up' instead. The grid isn't decoration; it's accident-prevention. Same on a screen.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The 7-13-22 Marketplace That Felt Cheap
blocks.source: Anonymous design lead at Bazaariya, a Hyderabad-based vernacular-first social commerce app
blocks.story:
Bazaariya raised a Series A on a thesis that *vibes matter in commerce*. Then they shipped a product where a single product card had **7px between the title and price, 13px between the price and the seller name, and 22px between the seller name and the rating**. No one had decided this. Three different designers had touched the card over four months, each eyeballing the spacing in Figma and shipping it.

The app worked. Users complained, but in vague, hard-to-action ways: *"feels janky,"* *"looks fake,"* *"don't trust it."* Post-purchase CSAT sat at **3.6 out of 5** for six straight months. The growth team blamed delivery. The PMs blamed the trust badges. A user-research session in October finally surfaced it: a focus group of 12 women in Hyderabad and Vijayawada used the word *sasta* — *cheap, badly-made* — about the visual feel. Nobody could explain *why*. They just felt it.

The design lead spent the next four weeks rebuilding every component on a strict **8-point grid** — 8, 16, 24, 32. Not 7. Not 13. Not 22. Same colours, same fonts, same illustrations. Shipped on December 14, 2024. **CSAT moved from 3.6 to 4.0 — twelve points up — within three weeks.** Nobody mentioned spacing. Several users said the app *"looked more professional now."* The design lead added one line to her year-end review: *"Standardised the spacing scale."*
blocks.takeaway: Users do not know what an 8-point grid is. They know when one is missing.

blocks.title: Vikram's Onboarding Flow
blocks.setup:
Two weeks into the **Saral Pay** engagement. Vikram emails you a Figma link at 11pm: *"I built the new onboarding myself over the weekend — 4 screens. Tell me what you think before standup tomorrow."*

You open it. The flow works. The copy is fine. But every screen has a different rhythm: the gap between the heading and the input on Screen 1 is **18px**. On Screen 2 it's **22px**. On Screen 3 it's **14px**. On Screen 4 it's **30px**. None of these are on any grid you can identify. Your job is to fix this without making Vikram feel attacked at 11pm.

coach.name: Design-Director Diya
coach.role: Your old boss. She invented the rule "never critique someone's spacing in writing after 9pm." You broke it once and learned.

stages.prompt: First decision: **how do you frame the feedback** when you reply to Vikram tonight?

options.label: "The spacing is all over the place — 18, 22, 14, 30. None of it is on a grid. Looks amateur."
options.explain: Accurate. Cruel. Vikram now thinks you think his work is amateur, which is the sentence he will remember from this engagement five years from now. Diya is mouthing *"god dammit"* at her phone.

options.label: "Looks great! Small tweak — let's standardise the vertical rhythm to an 8-point scale (8/16/24/32) so the four screens feel like one product. I'll send a redlined Figma in the morning."
options.explain: **This is the move.** You named the problem (rhythm), prescribed the system (8-point), and committed to a deliverable (redline). Vikram learns a vocabulary instead of an insult.

options.label: "Looks fine to me, ship it."
options.explain: He ships it. Two weeks later in user testing, three users use the word *sasta*. Vikram emails you at 11pm asking why his onboarding feels cheap. You now have to explain the thing you should have said the first time.

options.label: "Let's hop on a call tomorrow to walk through it."
options.explain: This is fine but defers the substance. Vikram will spend the next 14 hours wondering what's wrong. Worse, when you do call, you have no concrete prescription — just vague concern. Half-credit for not making it worse.

stages.prompt: Morning. You open Figma to redline. Heading-to-input gaps are **18, 22, 14, 30**. What's your **target spacing scale**?

options.label: **8, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64** — strict 8-point, with 4 as the half-step for tight typographic relationships.
options.explain: **Yes.** Six values cover 95% of cases. Multiples of 8 sit cleanly on most device pixel densities and make engineer handoff trivial. The 4-step half-step exists because text-baseline sometimes needs it.

options.label: **5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30** — a 5-point scale, easier mental math.
options.explain: Easier mental math, harder pixel hinting. 5-point scales drift on common screen densities and don't compose with the 8-point components most modern UI kits ship with. You introduced friction for everyone downstream to save yourself math.

options.label: **Whatever Figma's auto-layout suggests.**
options.explain: Figma's auto-layout doesn't suggest a scale; it accepts whatever you type. You just delegated the decision to the tool and it delegated it back to you. Now four screens have four different spacings *with auto-layout enabled*.

options.label: **Match Apple's HIG: 20pt margins, 16pt gutters.**
options.explain: HIG is iOS-platform guidance, not a generic spacing scale. Saral Pay ships on Android too, where the gestalt expectations are different. You picked one platform's rule and called it a system.

stages.prompt: Vikram pings: *"Why does the **section spacing** (between the heading block and the form block) need to be different from the **element spacing** (between the heading and its subhead)?"* Your answer?

options.label: "Because the gap is the relationship. Tight spacing says *these belong together*; loose spacing says *these are separate sections*. If section gap = element gap, the screen reads as one flat list."
options.explain: **Exactly.** Spacing is *information*. The 8-point step from 16 to 32 is the difference between *intra-group* and *inter-group*. Vikram now has language for *why* a system has multiple values, not just one.

options.label: "It just looks better that way — design intuition."
options.explain: Vikram cannot apply *intuition* the next time he opens Figma at 11pm on a weekend. You billed for vocabulary and delivered vibes. He will redo the spacing wrong on Screen 5.

options.label: "Material Design says so."
options.explain: Authority-by-citation works on no one, including Vikram. You also can't quote which page of MD says so, because you made it up. Diya is opening the *crying-emoji* keyboard shortcut.

options.label: "Because tighter inside, wider between — gestalt's law of proximity. Same principle that makes you read a paragraph as a paragraph and not as 47 floating words."
options.explain: **Solid.** Naming the principle gives Vikram a hook to remember it by. He will now over-cite *gestalt* in standups for the next month, but you've embedded a real concept.

stages.prompt: You finish the redline. Screen 1 is now **24px heading-to-input, 16px input-to-input, 48px section-to-section**. Vikram says: *"Should I just memorise these three numbers for every screen?"* Last call.

options.label: "No — memorise the *roles*. Element gap, group gap, section gap. Each role maps to a token (`space-2`, `space-3`, `space-6`). The values can change later; the roles shouldn't."
options.explain: **This is the move.** Tokens decouple intent from value. If you halve the app's overall density next year, you change three token values, not 400 instances. Vikram just learned how design systems actually work.

options.label: "Yes, just remember 16, 24, 48 and you'll be fine for everything."
options.explain: He will dutifully apply 16/24/48 to a marketing landing page and a transaction-confirmation screen alike. The numbers are right, the system is missing. Six months from now nothing will scale.

options.label: "Just always do 8x multiples — pick whatever feels right."
options.explain: *Whatever feels right* is exactly the rule that produced 18-22-14-30 last weekend. You're back where you started, with extra steps.

options.label: "I'll write a one-page spacing guide and put it in the Figma file."
options.explain: **Smart.** Documentation that lives in the file gets read; a Notion doc gets bookmarked and forgotten. One page, three roles, one example each. Vikram references it for the next 18 months.

outcomes.perfect: Vikram ships the new onboarding on a Tuesday. CSAT goes from 3.7 to 4.1 in three weeks. Nobody mentions spacing. He texts you: *"Engineering thanked me for the consistent spacing tokens."* **Diya nods, once.** This is the highest praise.
outcomes.good: You got the redline shipped but didn't quite land the token-vs-value distinction. Vikram will reinvent the system in six months. Re-read the lesson on **roles, not values**.
outcomes.learn: You either bruised the founder or shipped a flow that still feels jangly. Re-read the lesson — especially the section on **why an 8-point grid is a forcing function** for decisions you didn't realise you were making.

Pick 8 as your base unit. The math is the reason: clean halves, quarters, and pixel-perfect rendering.

lessons.subtitle: Type is a hierarchy of voices; color is a system of meanings

blocks.md:
Two design crimes happen on every junior team. The first: a designer picks 14 distinct font sizes 'because we need flexibility.' The second: an engineer pastes #FF0000 into the error toast component because Stack Overflow said red means error.

Both come from the same place — the absence of a system. With a system, type sizes get picked once for the whole product, and colour gets a name (`feedback-error`) before it gets a value (`#B91C1C`). Without a system, every screen is a fresh negotiation, and your product slowly looks like fourteen products.

blocks.md: Imagine your interface is a stage play. The H1 is the lead actor's line. The H2 is supporting cast. The body is dialogue. The caption is the stage direction nobody reads. **A type scale is the casting of voices for that play.** Six voices is a manageable cast; fourteen is a riot. Pick a ratio, derive the sizes, and refuse to add more without rewriting the whole script.

blocks.text: Move 1 — Pick a ratio, derive the scale

blocks.md:
A type scale is built by multiplying. Pick a base size (16px is the universal default for body text on web; the world has agreed) and a ratio. Each step in the scale is the previous step times the ratio.

The useful ratios for SaaS:

- **1.2 (minor third)** — subtle, dense, professional. Good for data-heavy dashboards.
- **1.25 (major third)** — the workhorse. Distinct enough to be hierarchical, calm enough to feel intentional.
- **1.333 (perfect fourth)** — louder. Marketing pages, content sites.
- **1.5 (perfect fifth)** — editorial. Long-form. Don't use this on a SaaS app unless you want every H1 to feel like a manifesto.

With a 1.25 ratio starting at 16: 16 → 20 → 24 → 32 → 40 → 48. Round to the nearest pixel; you don't need to be precious. Six steps is plenty for a SaaS app.

**Don't use seven.** The argument 'we need one between 20 and 24' is the start of cargo-cult typography. If you cannot decide between 20 and 24, the answer is to decide; not to add a 22.

blocks.title: Building a type scale from scratch in five minutes

steps.label: Step 1 — Set body size
steps.body: 16px on web. 17 on iOS-influenced apps. Don't overthink.

steps.label: Step 2 — Pick the ratio
steps.body: 1.25 for SaaS, 1.333 for marketing, 1.2 for dense data tools. If you can't decide, ship 1.25.

steps.label: Step 3 — Generate 5-6 sizes
steps.body: Multiply, round to nearest pixel. Stop at 5-6; one for each H level plus body and caption.

steps.label: Step 4 — Name them semantically
steps.body: text-display, text-h1, text-h2, text-h3, text-body, text-caption. Numbers are tempting; names survive a redesign.

steps.label: Step 5 — Document the line-heights
steps.body: Use a separate scale for line-height: 1.5 for body, 1.3 for headings. The single biggest readability lever you have.

blocks.prompt: Why is a 1.25 ratio more defensible than hand-picking each font size?

choices.label: Because each step is mathematically distinct from the one before, so hierarchy is automatic
choices.explain: A constant ratio means the visual jump between steps is predictable. The hierarchy is built into the math, not negotiated per-screen.

choices.label: Because 1.25 is what Material Design uses
choices.explain: It happens to be common, but the reason is the math, not the brand.

choices.label: Because designers who use ratios are taken more seriously
choices.explain: Status arguments aren't engineering arguments. The reason is the consistency, not the optics.

choices.label: Because 1.25 ratio renders faster in browsers
choices.explain: Browsers don't care about your ratio. The performance angle is irrelevant.

blocks.md:
Hex codes are technical debt. Every #3B82F6 you paste into a component is a future bug — when the brand changes, when dark mode lands, when accessibility fails, when a designer 'tweaks' it to #3D80F4 in one screen and forgets to update the others.

The fix is **design tokens**: named values you reference everywhere.

A minimal palette to start with:

- `surface-primary` — the page background.
- `surface-elevated` — cards, modals, popovers.
- `text-primary` — main reading copy.
- `text-muted` — secondary, captions.
- `interaction-default` — primary CTA fill.
- `interaction-hover` — primary CTA on hover.
- `feedback-error`, `feedback-warning`, `feedback-success` — status states.
- `border-default` — your one default border colour.

Notice these names are about **meaning**, not about colour. `interaction-default` could be navy in one product and orange in another — the components don't change. When the brand rebrand happens (it always happens), you change the value in one file and ship.

**Never use a token name that says the colour.** `blue-500` is the wrong abstraction; `interaction-default` is the right one. The day you decide your brand is no longer blue, you don't want to grep your codebase.

coach.name: Studio-Lead Saanvi
coach.role: design lead, 9 years across India and Singapore

intro: Type and colour today. Let me show you six choices teams make on a token system.
Tell me whether each is a good token name, a bad token name, or fine but missing context.

scenarios.situation: `color-blue-500`
scenarios.explain: Names the colour, not the meaning. The day your brand goes orange, every reference is wrong.

scenarios.situation: `interaction-default`
scenarios.explain: Names the role. Survives a rebrand. Lets dark mode swap the value cleanly.

scenarios.situation: `text-primary`
scenarios.explain: Generic but meaningful. Pairs cleanly with `text-muted` and `text-inverse`.

scenarios.situation: `navy-button-bg`
scenarios.explain: Encodes both the colour (navy) and the use (button-bg). Both bits will betray you eventually.

scenarios.situation: `bg`
scenarios.explain: Acceptable shorthand if the system has only one bg. The day you have multiple surfaces, you'll regret the lack of suffix.

scenarios.situation: `semantic-error-100` and `semantic-error-700`
scenarios.explain: Tiered semantic tokens are great — light fill for backgrounds, dark fill for text. The 100/700 maps to lightness, not absolute values.

blocks.caption: Watch the trap happen live — and the fix at the end.

blocks.title: The classic trap: branding the token names
blocks.md: Junior designers love naming tokens after the brand: `mahindra-orange`, `swiggy-red`, `paytm-blue`. It feels personal. It is also a guaranteed rebrand catastrophe. **Never name a token after a colour or a brand. Name it after the role it plays.** `interaction-default` could be navy today and saffron next year; `paytm-blue` is just a lie waiting to be found.

blocks.prompt: Order these steps for setting up a token system on a new product.

items.label: List the semantic categories you need
items.detail: surface, text, interaction, feedback, border. Five buckets cover most apps.

items.label: Pick 2-3 tokens per category
items.detail: Don't ship surface-1 through surface-9 on day one. Start with the ones you actually use.

items.label: Assign hex values to each token
items.detail: Pick the values once; this is the only place hex codes should live.

items.label: Wire tokens into Tailwind config or CSS variables
items.detail: Make the token names usable in code: bg-surface-elevated, text-text-muted.

items.label: Migrate one surface end-to-end
items.detail: Start with the most-used screen. Write down the leftover hex codes that still need a home.

blocks.hint: Think semantic categories first; hex values come last.

blocks.instruction: Define a minimum token set for a small Indian SaaS dashboard. Write 6-8 token names with their semantic role. Don't include hex values; this is the naming exercise. Defend each name in one short sentence.
blocks.expected: 1. surface-primary — the page background, used on the body. 2. surface-elevated — cards, modals, popovers; gives them visible separation from the page. 3. text-primary — main reading copy. 4. text-muted — captions, helper text, timestamps. 5. interaction-default — primary CTA fill; the only filled brand colour on a screen. 6. interaction-hover — slightly darker shade for the hover state of interaction-default. 7. feedback-error — error states across toasts, banners, inline validation. 8. border-default — the single default border for inputs, cards, and dividers, so dividers don't drift across components.

blocks.prompt: Which two of these are real reasons to use semantic tokens instead of hex codes? (pick two)

choices.label: Rebrands cost one diff instead of hundreds
choices.explain: Semantic tokens decouple the meaning from the value. One file changes; everything else inherits.

choices.label: Dark mode requires fewer overrides
choices.explain: If components reference `surface-elevated`, dark mode just remaps the value of that token. Components don't change.

choices.label: Hex codes render slower in browsers
choices.explain: There is no rendering cost. The cost is human, in maintenance and consistency.

choices.label: Designers prefer Figma's colour-style API
choices.explain: True but tangential. The reason isn't the tool; it's the abstraction.

hi-IN.title: Saree shop ka colour system
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, ek successful saree shop owner se baat ki. Bola — 'mein kabhi colour ka naam nahi rakhta — saari ko sirf woh shade kehta hu jo mood describe karta hai. Bridal-red, summer-cotton-blue, festive-gold. Customer shade nahi puchti, mood puchti hai.'

Design tokens isi ka coded version hai. Hex code shade hai; token name mood hai.

en.title: Same point, no saree shop
en.md: A successful saree-shop owner names every colour by mood, not by hex. 'Bridal red', 'monsoon blue', 'festive gold'. Customers don't ask for shades; they ask for moods. Tokens are the developer version of the same trick.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The 47 Hex Codes That Broke Dark Mode
blocks.source: Anonymous staff designer at NiyamPay, a Mumbai-based corporate-cards fintech
blocks.story:
NiyamPay shipped dark mode on **June 11, 2024**, after eight months of design work and a lot of internal congratulation. By **June 13**, three customers had filed bug reports about *invisible* receipts in the expense-approvals queue: white text on near-white background. By **June 17**, the engineering lead pulled the dark-mode rollout entirely.

The root cause, traced over a six-hour war-room: the design files contained **47 distinct hex codes for the colour grey**. `#F4F4F4`, `#F5F5F5`, `#F4F5F6`, `#F2F2F4`, and so on. No one — not the original designer, who had left in March — knew which grey was supposed to be `background-secondary` versus `surface-elevated` versus `divider-subtle`. The dark-mode build had been done by mapping each hex code to a single dark equivalent, but because the *intent* of each grey had never been recorded, several got mapped wrong. The receipt background and the receipt text got mapped to the same value.

The rebuild took eleven weeks. The team replaced every hex literal with **34 semantic tokens** (`bg-primary`, `bg-elevated`, `text-primary`, `text-muted`, `border-subtle`, etc.) and shipped dark mode again on **September 4, 2024**. Reported colour-related bugs in the next quarter dropped **85%** vs the same period the previous year. The new staff designer added a single rule to the design-system README: *"If you typed a hex code, you owe an explanation."*
blocks.takeaway: A hex code records what something looks like. A token records what something *is*. Only one of those survives a re-skin.

blocks.title: Vikram Wants a Brand Color
blocks.setup:
Six weeks into the **Saral Pay** engagement. Vikram's cofounder, who handles marketing, wants to add a **"festive saffron"** colour for an upcoming Diwali campaign — buttons, badges, the splash screen, *"maybe the whole top nav for the week."* Vikram forwards this to you with a single sentence: *"Need your help. He wants the hex code by EOD."*

It is 2:47pm. Your job is to keep the Diwali campaign from breaking the design system that you spent the last month establishing.

coach.name: Design-Director Diya
coach.role: Has personally watched four startups paint themselves into a corner with seasonal colours

stages.prompt: First decision. Vikram's cofounder wants `#FF6F00` everywhere for Diwali week. **What's your opening question to Vikram?**

options.label: "What is the **role** of this colour — is it a brand-accent, a campaign-flag, a CTA-replacement, or a notification-tone? Each one means a different decision."
options.explain: **Right question.** Naming the role first prevents `#FF6F00` from showing up in three contradictory places — like *both* a primary CTA *and* a destructive-action warning, which has happened to actual fintechs.

options.label: "What's the hex code? I'll add it."
options.explain: You just became a colour-vending machine. The cofounder gives you `#FF6F00` and you put it everywhere with no semantic anchor. Two weeks after Diwali, nobody remembers why the *Delete Account* button is festive saffron.

options.label: "Don't do it. Brand colours shouldn't change for seasons."
options.explain: You just told the cofounder *no* without offering a yes. He'll do it himself, badly. You're now both excluded from the decision and responsible for the outcome.

options.label: "Sure, but only on the splash screen — nowhere else."
options.explain: Arbitrary scope-limit with no principle behind it. The cofounder will negotiate it back up to four screens by Friday because you didn't anchor *why*.

stages.prompt: Vikram replies: *"He says it's a 'campaign accent' — show users it's Diwali, drive seasonal urgency."* You now know the role. **What's the right token strategy?**

options.label: Add a new token `accent-campaign-diwali-2026` mapped to `#FF6F00`. Use *only* in campaign components. Set an expiry comment in the file: `// remove after 2026-11-15`.
options.explain: **This is the move.** Scoped name, scoped use, scoped lifetime. The token can't accidentally leak into the design system because its name disqualifies it from anything that isn't a Diwali component. The expiry comment is the kill-switch.

options.label: Override `accent-primary` to `#FF6F00` for Diwali week, then change it back.
options.explain: Now every component using `accent-primary` — *including the Send Money button* — turns saffron. Users see a Diwali-coloured CTA on the *Block Card* destructive screen too. You broke the semantic layer to save 30 seconds.

options.label: Hardcode `#FF6F00` directly into the four campaign components.
options.explain: Six months from now someone will refactor those components and lose the hex. Or worse: the cofounder asks for a different shade and you have to find every literal. You traded a small upfront cost for a guaranteed future cleanup.

options.label: Add a new permanent `accent-festive` token, since festivals come every year.
options.explain: Plausible-sounding mistake. *Festive* is an aesthetic, not a role. Diwali, Holi, Christmas, and Eid all want different colours, and a single `accent-festive` will end up meaning one of them and breaking the others.

stages.prompt: Vikram pushes back: *"This feels like overkill. Why can't I just put the hex code in the file? It's one week."* **Your one-paragraph defence?**

options.label: "Because every hex you type is a future bug. The token has a name, a scope, and an expiry. The hex has none of those — and in three months the next person will see `#FF6F00` and have no idea if it's a brand colour, a warning, or a leftover."
options.explain: **Land it.** You named the cost (future bug), the asymmetry (named vs anonymous), and the human consequence (next person's confusion). Vikram nods.

options.label: "Because that's the rule."
options.explain: Vikram is the kind of founder who breaks rules he doesn't understand. *"That's the rule"* survives until 11pm Thursday when he opens Figma and types the hex anyway.

options.label: "Because Apple does it that way."
options.explain: Apple has a 200-person design-systems team. Saral Pay has you. The argument is structurally true and rhetorically lazy.

options.label: "Because if we ever need dark mode, every hex code will need to be re-thought from scratch — but every token already has a slot waiting for its dark-mode partner."
options.explain: **Sharp.** You connected today's micro-decision to a real future need (dark mode is on Vikram's roadmap for Q4). The token argument now sells itself.

stages.prompt: Vikram's convinced. Last decision: **how does this token live in the codebase?**

options.label: Add to `tailwind.config.ts` under `colors.accent.campaignDiwali2026`, with a code comment linking to the design doc and the kill-date. Reference it in components as `bg-accent-campaign-diwali-2026`.
options.explain: **Clean.** Lives in one place, queryable by grep, removable by deleting one line. Future-you will thank present-you. Diya is, momentarily, satisfied.

options.label: Add it to a new file `seasonal-colors.ts` separate from the main config.
options.explain: Now you have two sources of truth. The next designer will inevitably duplicate or forget about one of them. *Seasonal* is not a separate axis from *colour*; it's a property of one.

options.label: Just inline `#FF6F00` in the Diwali components for now and document it in the PR description.
options.explain: PR descriptions are write-once read-zero. The hex will live in the codebase for 18 months, untraceable. You undid the entire previous stage.

options.label: Add it as a CSS custom property `--diwali-2026: #FF6F00;` in the global stylesheet.
options.explain: **Also valid** if your stack relies on CSS vars. Same shape — named, scoped, queryable, deletable. The principle, not the syntax, is what matters.

outcomes.perfect: Diwali week ships. Saffron lives on the splash and one campaign card. On November 15, you delete one line and it's gone. The cofounder loved it. **Diya sends you a single thumbs-up emoji**, which is the maximum she gives.
outcomes.good: You got the token in, but the scoping is loose enough that some saffron leaked to a screen it shouldn't have. Not a disaster; flag it for the post-campaign cleanup. Re-read the section on **role-naming**.
outcomes.learn: Either Vikram ended up with `#FF6F00` hardcoded in four files, or `accent-primary` itself got overridden and broke half the app for a week. Re-read the lesson — especially **why a token records intent and a hex records appearance**, and only intent survives the second use case.

points: Pick a type-scale ratio (1.25 for SaaS) and derive 5-6 sizes. Six voices, not fourteen.
Body text on web is 16px. Anything below 14 is hostile to anyone over 35.
Line-height is the single biggest readability lever. 1.5 for body, 1.3 for headings.
Hex codes are technical debt. Use semantic tokens (interaction-default, feedback-error) so rebrands cost one diff.
Never name a token after a colour or brand. Name it after the role it plays.

lessons.title: Interaction Design and Microcopy
lessons.subtitle: Every click is a question; every state change is the answer

blocks.md:
Most interfaces are silent. You click, and you wait, and you wonder: did it hear you? Is something happening? Did I press the right thing? Should I press it again?

The shipping bug is rarely the slow API; it's that the UI gives no signal during the slow API. The fix is not engineering; it's interaction design — a 30-line state machine and a few lines of microcopy that turn a silent button into a conversation. By the end of this lesson you'll know how to design state transitions that confirm, and microcopy that defuses the user's anxiety in real time.

blocks.title: Mental model: every click is a question
blocks.md: When the user clicks, they are asking the interface a question: 'did this work?' The interface owes them an answer **inside 100 milliseconds**. Anything slower than that feels broken even if it isn't. The answer doesn't have to be the result; it just has to be acknowledgement that the question was heard. **A spinner inside 100ms is not a delay; it is a reply.**

blocks.caption: Watch a button transition through idle → hover → pressed → loading → success — five states, each with a job.

hi-IN.title: Auto-rickshaw meter wala lesson
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, Mumbai ki auto le. Driver ne meter daala — TRRR — sound aaya, screen blink hua. Ab tum chill ho. Kyunki tumhe pata hai meter chal raha hai. Ab dusri auto ke liye driver bola 'meter daal diya hai bhai' lekin koi sound nahi, koi blink nahi. Tumhe pure ride trust nahi hota.

UI mein same. State change is the meter sound. Bina iske, every interaction feels like a 'trust me bro' from the driver.

en.title: Same point, no auto
en.md: When the rickshaw meter clicks and beeps, you trust it. When the driver just says 'meter is on', you don't. State change is the audible-meter version of UI. Without it, every click is a 'trust me bro'.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · Loading states ladder — 4 escalating loading states by duration.

blocks.md:
Every interactive element should have **at least five states**, each visually distinct:

1. **Idle** — the rest state.
2. **Hover** — slight elevation or colour shift; signals 'this is interactive'.
3. **Pressed** — depressed or darker; signals 'I heard you'.
4. **Loading** — spinner, shimmer, or skeleton; signals 'I'm working'.
5. **Success or Error** — explicit confirmation; signals 'here is what happened'.

Most junior designers ship two: idle and hover. Some skip hover entirely. The user is then forced to guess at every interaction whether the system is alive.

The useful version of this rule: **anything that takes more than 200 milliseconds to respond needs a loading state, and anything that takes more than 2 seconds needs progress indication, not just a spinner.** A spinner that runs forever is more anxiety-inducing than no spinner at all. If you can show a percentage, a step counter, or a 'this usually takes 5 seconds' message, do it.

For the result state: a quiet inline confirmation beats a modal toast for routine actions; a celebration beats a quiet confirmation for a milestone (first invoice sent, first user invited). Match the volume of the feedback to the importance of the action.

blocks.title: Designing the lifecycle of a single button click

steps.label: T+0ms — Click registered
steps.body: Button enters pressed state immediately. Visual shift: slightly darker fill, slight depression. Cost: 10 lines of CSS.

steps.label: T+50ms — Optimistic state
steps.body: If the action is safe to assume success (a like, a star, a non-destructive toggle), update the UI immediately. Roll back on error.

steps.label: T+200ms — Loading kicks in
steps.body: If the request hasn't returned yet, swap label to 'Saving…' and add a spinner. Disable the button to prevent double-click.

steps.label: T+2000ms — Progress indication
steps.body: If still pending after 2s, change copy to 'Still working… this usually takes a few seconds.' Anxiety drops; abandonment drops.

steps.label: T+resolved — Result state
steps.body: Inline 'Saved' for routine; toast for cross-page actions; modal celebration only for genuine milestones. Match volume to importance.

blocks.prompt: Your 'Send invoice' button has a 1.4 second backend roundtrip. Users are double-clicking and getting duplicate invoices. The fix is:

choices.label: Add an immediate pressed-state, swap to 'Sending...' inside 200ms, and disable the button until the request resolves
choices.explain: The pressed-state answers 'did you hear me?' inside 100ms; the loading state owns the next 1.4 seconds; disable kills the double-click. Three lines of UI logic, one solved problem.

choices.label: Speed up the backend to under 200ms
choices.explain: Worth doing eventually, but the perceived-responsiveness fix is in the UI. Backend optimisation takes a sprint; the UI fix takes ten minutes.

choices.label: Add a confirmation modal before sending
choices.explain: Adds a click. Solves intent confirmation, not the unresponsive feeling. The double-clicks would still happen if the modal is also slow.

choices.label: Show a toast 'Invoice sent' when the request resolves
choices.explain: Useful for the success state, but the silent 1.4 seconds is the actual bug. The toast is what comes after the loading state, not instead of it.

hi-IN.title: Paytm ka tring sound
hi-IN.md:
Paytm ne ek genius move kiya tha — successful payment ke baad 'tring' sound aur green tick. Shopkeeper ko phone dekhne ki bhi zaroorat nahi, kaan se sun lo. Yeh state change ka peak design hai — auditory + visual + emotional confirmation, sab ek time pe.

Aaj UPI apps mein yeh sound hai matlab interaction is solved. Bina iski har payment 'gaya kya?' wala question reh jaata.

en.title: Same point, no Paytm
en.md: Paytm's success-tring sound is a perfect interaction-design move: auditory plus visual plus emotional confirmation, all delivered inside 200ms. The shopkeeper doesn't even have to look at the phone. State change at its loudest is sometimes the right call.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · Confirmation hierarchy — Toast vs modal vs full-page.

blocks.md:
Microcopy is every word in your interface that isn't the brand name or the body content. Buttons, labels, error messages, empty states, tooltips, placeholders, modal titles, system notifications. They are the single largest unowned design surface in most products.

Three principles, in order of impact:

1. **Name the verb.** Buttons should say what the user is doing. 'Save invoice' beats 'Save'. 'Send password reset link' beats 'Submit'. The user is performing an action; the button is the noun-verb.

2. **Errors should name the cause.** 'Something went wrong' is the apology of a system that doesn't know what happened. 'We couldn't save your invoice — your card was declined; try a different card or contact your bank' is twelve more words and infinitely more useful. The user can act on cause; they cannot act on apology.

3. **Empty states are onboarding.** A blank screen with 'No invoices yet' is a wasted moment. The same screen with 'No invoices yet — your invoices will appear here as you create them. Click below to make your first one.' converts new users at 3-4x the rate. The empty state is the most persuasive surface in your product because the user has nothing else to look at.

A crisp test: read every piece of microcopy in your product out loud. If it sounds like a 1990s government form, rewrite it.
