coach.name: Studio-Lead Saanvi
coach.role: design lead, 9 years across India and Singapore

intro: Microcopy and interaction today. I'll show you six bits of copy or interaction patterns from real-ish apps.
Tell me whether each one helps the user, hurts them, or is technically fine but missing a chance.

scenarios.situation: An empty inbox screen showing only a sad cloud illustration and the text 'No emails.'
scenarios.explain: Empty states are the best onboarding moment in your app. Use them to show what would appear and how to get there.

scenarios.situation: A 'Submit' button on a contact form.
scenarios.explain: Submit is institutional. 'Send message' is the verb the user is doing.

scenarios.situation: An error toast: 'Network error. Code: ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432.'
scenarios.explain: Exposing a stack trace to the user is hostile. Translate technical errors into plain English with a useful next step.

scenarios.situation: A primary CTA that says 'Pay Rs.2,400 now'.
scenarios.explain: Names the verb (pay), the amount (Rs.2,400), and the urgency (now). The user knows exactly what will happen on click.

scenarios.situation: A delete-account dialog asks the user to type their email to confirm.
scenarios.explain: Friction matched to the cost. Destructive irreversible actions deserve more friction; trivial ones don't.

scenarios.situation: A loading spinner that has been spinning for 8 seconds with no progress text.
scenarios.explain: Anxiety grows with time. After 2 seconds, swap to 'Still working — this usually takes a few seconds.' Even fake progress beats silent spin.

blocks.caption: Watch the trap happen live — and the fix at the end.

blocks.title: The classic trap: copying the placeholder
blocks.md: Junior teams ship microcopy that started life as Lorem Ipsum and got 'good enough' replacement text in week six. Three months later the dashboard's empty state still reads 'Welcome to dashboard' and the error message still says 'An error occurred.' **Microcopy is not done when it is grammatically correct; it is done when it does a job.** The job is to defuse user anxiety, name the next step, or convert a blank screen into onboarding. If your copy doesn't do one of those, rewrite it.

blocks.prompt: Order these from highest to lowest impact when auditing microcopy for the first time.

items.label: Empty states
items.detail: The single most persuasive surface in the product because users have nothing else to look at.

items.label: Error messages
items.detail: Bad errors train learned helplessness; good ones convert errors into recovery.

items.label: Primary CTAs across all screens
items.detail: Generic verbs (Submit, OK) cost conversion at every step in the funnel.

items.label: Form labels and helper text
items.detail: Labels and helper text remove the guesswork on what each field expects.

items.label: Tooltips and inline tips
items.detail: Lower-impact polish layer. Important, but only after the structural copy is right.

blocks.hint: Start where users get most stuck.

blocks.instruction: Rewrite this generic error message for a small Bengaluru SaaS that sells expense management: 'An error occurred while processing your request. Please try again later.' Write a version that names the cause (assume it was a network timeout), names the next step, and matches the voice of a calm, opinionated product. 2-3 sentences max.
blocks.expected: We couldn't save your expense — looks like the network dropped before we got it to the server. Your data is still on this screen, so you can try again without re-typing. If this keeps happening, your office WiFi is the most likely culprit; switch to mobile data and retry.

blocks.prompt: Which two are characteristics of good error microcopy? (pick two)

choices.label: Names the cause when the system can identify it
choices.explain: Cause is actionable; apology is not. The user wants to know what happened and what to do next.

choices.label: Suggests a concrete next step
choices.explain: Even 'try again in a minute' is better than a dead-end. Errors are recovery moments, not endings.

choices.label: Includes the technical error code in plain text
choices.explain: Stack traces and error codes are for the support inbox, not the user. Translate them.

choices.label: Apologises profusely to soften the blow
choices.explain: Profuse apology signals 'we knew this would happen and shipped it anyway.' Calm and specific beats sorry-sorry-sorry every time.

hi-IN.title: Bank ka SMS wala genius
hi-IN.md:
ICICI ya HDFC ka transaction SMS dekha hai? 'Rs.2,400 debited from A/c XX1234 to ZOMATO via UPI on 5-May. Ref: 234524.' Sab kuch ek line mein — amount, account, payee, channel, date, ref. Yeh microcopy ka peak hai. Koi 'transaction successful' generic message nahi, sab data jo user ko chahiye, sab there.

Aur error wala SMS bhi same — 'Insufficient balance' nahi, 'Insufficient balance — current balance Rs.842, requires Rs.2,400.' Cause + diagnosis + fix, sab inline.

en.title: Same point, no SMS
en.md: Indian bank transaction SMSes are accidentally great microcopy. Every line tells you the amount, the account, the payee, the channel, the date, and a reference. No 'transaction successful' fluff. The error SMSes follow the same pattern — cause plus diagnosis plus fix. Steal the format.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The 3.4 Buy Buttons Per Checkout
blocks.source: Anonymous product designer at MetroBites, a Chennai-based quick-commerce food delivery app
blocks.story:
MetroBites had a payment-confirmation problem nobody had a name for. The technical metric the engineering team watched was *retry rate*: how often a single user tapped the **Pay ₹** button more than once on the same order. The number, in late 2024, was **3.4 taps on average**. Some users tapped seven times. The payment infra was billed per attempted transaction; this alone cost the company **₹14 lakh a month** in extra gateway fees, before counting the support load.

The root cause was a 3.2-second delay between tap and any visible response. The screen sat there. No spinner. No state change on the button. No copy. Users — entirely reasonably — assumed the tap hadn't registered, and tapped again. And again. Then a third time, this time *harder*, as if the screen could feel desperation.

The redesign shipped on **January 22, 2025**: an optimistic UI pattern where the button immediately changed to a disabled state with a spinner and the copy *"Confirming with your bank..."*, paired with a small line below — *"This usually takes 2-4 seconds."* The actual confirmation latency did not change. The interaction redesign took a senior designer four hours including the copy reviews.

Retries dropped **73%** in the first two weeks. Gateway fees fell by **₹10.2 lakh in February**. Customer support tickets tagged *"payment failed but money debited"* dropped from 312 to 41 a week. The CFO mentioned it on the next earnings call, attributed it to *"engineering improvements."*
blocks.takeaway: If your interface goes silent during the hardest 3 seconds of a user's day, they will not assume it is working.

blocks.title: Vikram's Payment Confirmation
blocks.setup:
Eight weeks into the **Saral Pay** engagement. Vikram is wiring up the new Send Money flow and hits the same wall every fintech hits: the bank's confirmation API takes between **1.8 and 4.5 seconds** to respond. He pings you: *"What do I show during that gap? Engineering wants to know if a spinner is enough."*

You know it isn't.

coach.name: Design-Director Diya
coach.role: Once made a deck called 'Loading States Are a Design Problem, Not an Engineering One.' Has shown it 47 times.

stages.prompt: Vikram's first proposal: **"Just put a spinner in the middle of the screen and grey out the button. Standard pattern."** What do you push back with?

options.label: "A spinner alone is decoration. The user needs three things: confirmation that the tap registered, a sense of *what* is happening, and a sense of *how long*. A spinner gives one of three."
options.explain: **Yes.** You named the user's three latent questions. *Did it register? What's happening? How long?* Every loading state worth shipping answers all three.

options.label: "Spinners are fine for short waits. But 4.5 seconds is long, so use a progress bar instead."
options.explain: Progress bar implies determinism. Bank APIs are non-deterministic — sometimes 1.8s, sometimes 4.5s. Your bar will sit at 80% for 3 seconds and users will think it's stuck. You traded one bad signal for another.

options.label: "Sure, ship it."
options.explain: MetroBites's CFO is currently writing your eulogy. Vikram ships, retries spike, gateway costs balloon, and three weeks from now he asks you why payment volume is fine but margin is shrinking.

options.label: "Add a fun animation — keep users entertained while they wait."
options.explain: Users are not bored, they are *anxious about whether they just sent ₹50,000 to the wrong UPI ID.* A dancing rupee symbol is condescending. Diya is making the *no* hand gesture from across the room.

stages.prompt: You convince Vikram. Now: **what does the button itself do** the moment the user taps?

options.label: Button instantly changes to a disabled state with an inline spinner *and* the copy `Confirming...`. Stays in place — does not jump.
options.explain: **This is the move.** Optimistic UI: act immediately, narrate quietly, don't move the screen around. The user gets feedback inside the 100ms window the brain treats as *cause and effect*.

options.label: Button disappears; a full-screen modal slides up with `Processing your payment`.
options.explain: You broke the spatial relationship between cause (tap) and effect (response). Users now wonder if the button broke. Modals are also expensive to dismiss if something goes wrong — you're now two screens deep in an error.

options.label: Button stays the same; a small spinner appears next to it.
options.explain: If the button still looks tappable, users will tap again to be sure. You spent two stages avoiding this exact failure and re-enabled it.

options.label: Button becomes a circular progress indicator that fills clockwise.
options.explain: Same problem as the progress bar — implies determinism you don't have. Also: the circular fill takes longer than 4.5 seconds visually if you make it smooth, so users see it *finish* before the API responds. Now they're confused *and* frustrated.

stages.prompt: The button is handled. Vikram asks: **"What about the copy? Engineering said `Loading...` is fine."** What microcopy do you ship?

options.label: **`Confirming with your bank... usually 2 to 4 seconds`** — names *who* is doing the work, sets a *time expectation*, no full stop.
options.explain: **Strong.** *Confirming with your bank* externalises the wait — it's the bank's slowness, not yours. *2 to 4 seconds* sets a rough expectation without overpromising. Users will tolerate twice the wait if you tell them the wait exists.

options.label: **`Loading...`** — minimal, doesn't make promises.
options.explain: *Loading* is a developer word, not a human word. It also tells the user nothing they don't already know from the spinner. You used three letters of screen real estate to add zero information.

options.label: **`Please wait while we process your transaction. Do not refresh or close this page.`** — explicit and safe.
options.explain: Banking-portal energy from 2007. Long, defensive, unfriendly, and the *do not close* warning *creates* the anxiety it's trying to prevent. Users will now panic-tap.

options.label: **`Hold tight! ✨ We're working some magic with your bank ✨`** — friendly and warm.
options.explain: The user is sending money. They want competence, not whimsy. The sparkle emojis on a transaction screen will make a 45-year-old uncle close the app and call you. Diya has stopped responding to your pings.

stages.prompt: Vikram asks the final question: **"What if the bank takes more than 4 seconds? Or fails?"** This is the failure-mode microcopy. What do you ship?

options.label: At 5s, copy switches to `Taking longer than usual — we will not double-charge you.` On hard failure: `Payment did not go through. No money was deducted. Try again or use a different method.`
options.explain: **Lands it.** The 5-second copy preempts the *exact* fear that drives multi-tap ("will I be charged twice?"). The failure copy names the consequence (`No money was deducted`) before offering the action. Both written in human language.

options.label: At 5s, show a spinner forever and hope it resolves.
options.explain: Users will close the app, reopen it, and find their money in limbo. Support tickets will spike. You're back to MetroBites's ₹14 lakh problem, just with a nicer button.

options.label: On failure: `Error 500: Payment gateway timeout. Please try again later.`
options.explain: Engineer copy. Users do not know what 500 means and do not care. They want to know: *is my money gone?* Tell them that or you've failed at the only thing the screen had to do.

options.label: Add a `Cancel` link below the spinner that the user can tap if they get worried.
options.explain: **Smart secondary.** Even if cancel doesn't actually stop the API call (it can't, after a certain point), the *option to escape* dramatically reduces anxiety. Pair this with the 5-second copy switch and you've covered both axes.

outcomes.perfect: Saral Pay's new Send Money ships in week 9. Vikram emails the team after the first week of data: *"Retries down 68%, support tickets for 'didn't go through' down 80%."* You quietly celebrate. **Diya sends one word: 'good.'**
outcomes.good: You got the optimistic UI right but one of the copy lines is doing too much (or too little) work. Real users will mostly forgive you. Re-read the section on **how microcopy answers the user's actual fears**, not the developer's mental model.
outcomes.learn: Either users still feel the wait (because the button looks unchanged) or the copy made things worse. Re-read the lesson — especially the section on **the three latent questions** every loading state must answer in under 4 seconds.

points: Every click is a question. The interface owes the user an answer inside 100ms — even if the answer is just 'I heard you.'
Five button states (idle, hover, pressed, loading, success/error) are the minimum. Most teams ship two.
Anything over 200ms needs a loading state; anything over 2 seconds needs progress indication.
Microcopy: name the verb (Save invoice, not Submit), name the cause in errors, treat empty states as onboarding.
Match the volume of feedback to the importance of the action. A like is a colour change; a milestone deserves a celebration.

What is the longest the button can spin before the user gets anxious — and is your loading state actually distinct from the idle state?

lessons.title: The Design Feedback Loop
lessons.subtitle: Critique is the second design step, not the last

audioChapters.label: Mental model: critique is step two, not step ten

blocks.md:
Most teams treat design critique as the last gate before shipping. The designer pushes a Figma link to Slack, four people drop unstructured opinions in the thread, the loudest one wins, and the work goes back for a 'revision'. The cycle is slow, demoralising, and rarely produces better design — only different design.

The fix is not better Figma comments. It's a critique loop run early, structured, and goal-anchored. Three questions and one ritual fix the bulk of it. By the end of this lesson, you will run critiques that improve the work instead of just trading taste.

blocks.md: Treat critique as **step two of the design process, not step ten**. The job of the first sketch is to become wrong on purpose so a critique can pull it toward right. Designers who polish before critique waste polish; teams that critique only at the end produce design that is locally optimal and globally weird. **Make the cost of being wrong cheap by inviting critique while the work is still ugly.**

hi-IN.title: Mummy ka unboxing
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, naya design banaya. Thumb-up Slack pe daala. PM ne emoji react kiya. Founder ne 'looks great' kaha. Tu khush. Ab tu mummy ko phone pe screen dikhata hai. Mummy bolti hai — 'beta yeh button ka kya kaam hai?' Tu rukta hai.

Mummy critique single most underrated tool hai. Koi context nahi, koi politeness ki padding nahi. Sirf 'kya hai yeh?' Yahi sawal aapke design ka catch karta hai jo team kabhi nahi pakdegi.

en.title: Same point, no mummy
en.md: Show your design to your team and you'll get polite agreement. Show it to a person with no product context and they'll ask 'what does this button do?' That single question is the cheapest, harshest critique you can buy. Find your version of the mummy-test.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · Critique loop — See → judge → propose → iterate.

blocks.md:
Most critique fails because it has no structure. 'I don't like the colour' is not actionable; 'this could be cleaner' is not a critique, it's a vibe. The fix is to anchor every critique to three questions, in order:

1. **What is this screen's single most important action, and how do I know?**
If three reviewers give three different answers, the visual hierarchy is broken. This is the cheapest critique question in the world. It catches more design problems than the next ten questions combined.

2. **What would break if a user opened this with no context?**
The edge cases hide in the assumed context. The user lands on this screen from an email link, doesn't know what they're looking at, has no onboarding tour. What confuses them? What microcopy assumes too much? What state is missing — empty, loading, error?

3. **What would a cold reviewer push back on?**
Name the most likely critique a senior designer or skeptical engineer would make, before they make it. If you can't name one, you haven't pressure-tested the work yet. If you can name three, write them down and answer them in the PR description.

The order matters. Question 1 is structural; Question 2 is contextual; Question 3 is anticipatory. Done in order, they catch problems at decreasing levels of severity. Done out of order, you spend an hour debating button colours while the hierarchy is still broken.

blocks.title: Running a 15-minute critique using the 3-question loop

steps.label: Min 0-2 — Show the work cold
steps.body: No designer commentary, no walkthrough. Reviewers see the screen the way a user would. Silence is fine.

steps.label: Min 2-5 — Question 1: primary action
steps.body: Each reviewer points at what they think is the primary action. If you get more than one answer, you have a structural problem to fix before continuing.

steps.label: Min 5-9 — Question 2: cold context
steps.body: Pretend the user landed here from a deep link with no onboarding. Walk through what is unclear, missing, or assumed.

steps.label: Min 9-13 — Question 3: anticipated pushback
steps.body: Designer names the three most likely senior-design pushbacks. Reviewers add their own. Write them down.

steps.label: Min 13-15 — Decisions
steps.body: Three buckets: fix now, fix in next iteration, document and ship. No 'discuss further' — that's procrastination dressed up as care.

blocks.prompt: A teammate opens critique with 'I don't like the colour palette.' What is the most useful redirect?

choices.label: Ask: which goal does the colour fail — accessibility, hierarchy, brand, or emotion?
choices.explain: Critique without a goal is taste. Naming the goal turns the conversation into something you can act on or close.

choices.label: Defend the palette by quoting the brand guidelines
choices.explain: Defensive moves end critique loops; they don't improve them.

choices.label: Change the colour and move on
choices.explain: Changing without learning why guarantees the same critique on the next screen.

choices.label: Open a Figma comment thread to async the discussion
choices.explain: Async is fine, but it doesn't change the quality of the critique. The redirect to a goal is what matters.

hi-IN.title: Pune studio ka critique ritual
hi-IN.md:
Pune ke ek 6-person design studio mein har Friday 4pm critique. Designer ne sirf ek slide pe pre-fill karna hai — 'is screen ka primary action X hai, kyunki Y, aur main soch raha hu Z reviewer Q ke baare mein puchega.' 30 second me read hota hai, baaki 14 minutes me actual critique. Pehle jo 60 minute lagte the, ab 15 me khatam.

Pre-filled context = real critique time.

en.title: Same point, no Friday standup
en.md: A Pune studio runs a 15-minute weekly critique where the designer pre-fills one slide naming the primary action and the most likely pushback. Reviewers spend the saved 45 minutes on actual critique instead of decoding context. The format scales from 6 people to 60.

blocks.md:
When design moves to engineering, most teams lose half the work. The Figma file gets copy-pasted into components, the 'why' evaporates, and three sprints later nobody remembers why the modal was 480px wide instead of 520.

The fix is the **spec-first PR**: write the user-facing change in plain English at the top of the PR description, *before* the code review, and require it on every design-related PR. Three short paragraphs:

1. **What changed for the user.** One sentence. 'Onboarding now asks for company size on step 2 instead of step 4.'
2. **Why.** One short paragraph. 'Step 4 had a 31% drop-off; moving the question earlier lets us conditionally hide steps 5 and 6 for solo users.'
3. **What we're not doing.** One short paragraph. 'We're not changing the visual layout or the field validation; that's a separate PR.'

This costs the designer or engineer five extra minutes. It saves the reviewers an hour of figuring out intent from diff. It also means six months later, when someone wonders why step 2 has the company-size question, the answer is in the git history, not in a Slack thread that's been deleted.

The spec-first PR is the single highest-leverage ritual you can add to a design-engineering team. It's free, it's writable in any text box, and it kills the 'wait, why did we do this?' meeting before it gets scheduled.

intro: Last lesson, last scenarios. Today: critique moves you'll use in PRs and reviews.
Tell me whether each one makes the loop tighter, makes it longer, or has no effect at all.

scenarios.situation: A designer pushes a fully polished Figma file to Slack and asks for 'thoughts.'
scenarios.explain: Polish before critique wastes polish, and 'thoughts' invites unstructured taste. Always invite critique on rough work with specific questions.

scenarios.situation: A PR description that opens with 'What changed for the user' in one sentence.
scenarios.explain: The spec-first move. Reviewers can react to intent before parsing the diff. Saves rebase cycles.

scenarios.situation: A reviewer comments 'I don't like this' with no further explanation.
scenarios.explain: Critique without a goal is taste. The designer now has to guess what to fix, and probably guesses wrong.

scenarios.situation: Designer attaches a Loom video walking through every screen in the PR.
scenarios.explain: Videos can be useful but they're a substitute for written intent, and they're harder to grep later. Prefer the prose.

scenarios.situation: Reviewer asks 'what's the primary action on this screen?' before commenting on anything else.
scenarios.explain: Question 1 of the 3-question critique. Catches structural problems before everyone debates colour.

scenarios.situation: Critique meeting ends with 'let's discuss further async.'
scenarios.explain: Procrastination dressed up as care. End every critique with three buckets: fix now, fix later, document and ship.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the polish-before-critique cycle
blocks.md: Designers want to show finished work; reviewers want to be invited to opinion. So designers polish for two days, then 'open up critique' on a thing that is too pretty to change. Reviewers feel rude pointing at structural problems and instead trade taste on colour and copy. **The polished design is the enemy of the good design.** Invite critique while the work is sketchy and the changes are cheap. The polish layer is the last 10%, not the first 90%.

blocks.prompt: Order the steps to fix a stuck design critique loop on a small team.

items.label: Adopt the 3-question critique format
items.detail: Question 1, Question 2, Question 3, in that order, every time.

items.label: Make designers invite critique on rough sketches, not polished comps
items.detail: The norm has to shift from 'show your best' to 'show your draft'.

items.label: Require spec-first PR descriptions on design changes
items.detail: Three paragraphs: what changed, why, what we're not doing.

items.label: End every critique with explicit decisions, not 'let's discuss further'
items.detail: Three buckets: fix now, fix later, document and ship.

items.label: Document recurring critique themes in a team doc
items.detail: If the same critique keeps coming up, it's a system gap, not a screen gap. Fix the system.

blocks.hint: Start with the question structure; the rest follows.

blocks.instruction: Write the spec-first PR description for a small change: you've moved the 'Forgot password?' link from below the password field to above it, on the login screen of an Indian SaaS used by accountants. Three paragraphs: what changed, why, what you're NOT doing. 4-6 sentences total.
blocks.expected: **What changed:** The 'Forgot password?' link now sits directly above the password field instead of below it on the login screen. **Why:** Customer support tickets show that 18% of password-reset requests come from users who didn't notice the link below the field on their first scan. Putting it above moves it into the user's natural sight-line as they shift focus from email to password. **What we're not doing:** We're not changing the link's wording, the password field validation, or the visual hierarchy of the primary 'Sign in' button. Those are separate decisions that should be made on their own evidence.

blocks.prompt: Which two are signs your team's critique loop is healthy? (pick two)

choices.label: Designers regularly invite critique on rough sketches, not just polished comps
choices.explain: The earlier the critique, the cheaper the change. Sketch-stage critique is the highest-leverage moment.

choices.label: PR descriptions consistently name the user-facing change before the code
choices.explain: Spec-first PRs make intent reviewable. Reviewers can flag the intent before they read the diff.

choices.label: Critique meetings consistently overrun their 15-minute slot
choices.explain: Overrun signals lack of structure. A 15-minute critique that uses the 3-question funnel finishes on time and produces clearer decisions.

choices.label: Senior designers do most of the talking
choices.explain: Critique that depends on senior approval doesn't scale. Healthy loops produce clear pushback from anyone with structural questions.

hi-IN.title: Bollywood film ka first cut
hi-IN.md:
Bollywood mein editor pehle ek 'rough cut' banata hai — full film, sab scene, koi VFX nahi, koi colour grading nahi. Director, producer, star sab dekhte hain. Critique waise hi hota hai — kahaani level pe, character level pe. Phir polish hota hai.

UI mein bhi same. Pehle wireframe pe critique, phir visual pe, phir microcopy pe. Polished mockup pe 'kahaani' wala critique impossible hai — sab design ki taraf khinch jaate hain.

en.title: Same point, no movie
en.md: Bollywood editors run a rough-cut screening — full film, no VFX, no grading — to get story-level critique before polish. Same in UI: wireframe critique catches structure, visual critique catches polish, microcopy critique catches voice. Mix the layers up and you get unanchored taste.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Designer Who Skipped Critique
blocks.source: Anonymous design manager at PadhAI Tutor, a Gurugram-based AI-tutoring app for K-12
blocks.story:
PadhAI's Series-B launch event was scheduled for **October 8, 2024**. The lead designer on the new parent dashboard — call him R, three years out of NID, very confident — refused two scheduled critique sessions in the last sprint. *"Calls slow me down, the team will nitpick fonts, I've got it."* His manager, conflict-averse and slammed with hiring, let it slide both times.

Launch shipped on schedule. Within **72 hours**, three problems surfaced that any 30-minute critique would have caught: the *Add Child* CTA was below the fold on the most common Android screen size; the parent's weekly progress report used a colour scale where *red* meant *good* (mapped backward from a heatmap library); and the PIN-setup flow asked for the PIN *before* explaining what the PIN was for, leading to a **47% drop-off** at that screen.

The team shipped **three emergency redesigns over the next eleven days**. The first two were patches; the third was a full rebuild of the PIN flow. R was not fired but was moved off the dashboard team. His manager wrote a one-paragraph addendum to the team's working agreement: *"Critique is not feedback you opt into. It is the cheapest insurance you can buy on a deadline."*

The interesting part: R came back in February having internalised the lesson. By Q2 2025 he was running the team's critique sessions himself — including a rule that *every* design lead must present at least one half-finished file per sprint, *especially* when they think it doesn't need it. The team's launch-incident rate dropped to roughly one per quarter from one per launch.
blocks.takeaway: Critique is not a tax on confident designers. It is the only thing that turns a confident designer into a senior one.

blocks.title: Two Weeks to Launch
blocks.setup:
Twelve weeks into the **Saral Pay** engagement. The launch is in **two weeks**. Vikram pings you Monday morning: *"I know we planned a critique session this week but honestly we should just ship. Three new screens, all 90% there, can we just push?"*

You know what *just ship* means. Your job is to apply the **3-question critique** — *what is this trying to do? what is in the way? what is the smallest change that helps?* — to the three screens, and decide what gets cut so launch happens on time *and* doesn't blow up.

coach.name: Design-Director Diya
coach.role: Has personally been the *just ship* person. Has the scars.

stages.prompt: First decision: **how do you respond to Vikram's *"just ship"* message?**

options.label: "Two weeks is *more* reason to critique, not less. 90 minutes Wednesday — we walk through the three screens with the 3-question loop, decide what ships and what cuts. Faster than the redesign you'll need post-launch."
options.explain: **Right framing.** You re-anchored the cost: critique is cheaper than rework. You also gave a specific time-bounded ask (90 minutes Wednesday). Vikram says yes because the alternative he just proposed sounds vague.

options.label: "Sure, let's just ship. We'll iterate post-launch."
options.explain: Post-launch *iteration* is the polite name for *emergency hotfix at 11pm on launch day*. PadhAI did three of these in eleven days. You signed up to be on-call for whatever breaks.

options.label: "You're the founder, your call."
options.explain: You abdicated. The exact moment Vikram needed a contrary expert opinion, you became a yes-machine. Why is he paying you?

options.label: "Send me the Figma, I'll review async tonight and send notes."
options.explain: **Acceptable second-best.** Async critique loses the back-and-forth but preserves the actual review. Pair with one short call to discuss the highest-impact items. Half-credit because it works only if you actually send the notes by morning.

stages.prompt: Wednesday's call. **Screen 1**: a *Refer a Friend* feature with three reward tiers, illustrated badges, and a leaderboard. Vikram is excited about it. Apply question 1: ***"What is this trying to do?"***

options.label: Ask Vikram to state, in one sentence, what behaviour this screen is supposed to drive — and within how many days. If he can't, the screen is solving a vibe, not a problem.
options.explain: **The first question of any critique.** If the goal isn't crisp, no amount of design fixes the screen. Vikram pauses for a long moment and says: *"...we want users to invite people."* That's not a goal; that's the feature description.

options.label: Suggest moving the leaderboard above the badges for better visual hierarchy.
options.explain: You jumped to *what is in the way* before establishing *what it's trying to do*. You're polishing a screen that may not need to exist for launch.

options.label: Praise the illustrations — they're really nice.
options.explain: Critique is not a feedback sandwich. Compliments at the start of a critique are cortisol-suppressors that delay the substance. Diya's eye is twitching.

options.label: Ask if there's user research validating that referrals matter for Saral Pay's growth model right now.
options.explain: **Sharp.** This is the *what is this trying to do* question at the strategic layer. If referrals aren't a top-3 acquisition lever in month 1, the entire screen is a candidate for the cut list — illustrations and all.

stages.prompt: Vikram concedes Refer-a-Friend can wait. **Screen 2**: the *Onboarding KYC* flow, which works but has 7 steps. Apply question 2: ***"What is in the way?"*** What do you look for?

options.label: Drop-off cliffs between steps; fields the user can't answer without leaving the app; copy that sounds like compliance not a person; any step that re-asks something already given.
options.explain: **Lands it.** *In the way* is concrete: friction the user can name. Naming four candidates lets you and Vikram walk the screens looking for them. You find that step 4 asks for PAN *and* DOB on separate screens (re-ask), and step 6 asks for *occupation* with 47 dropdown options.

options.label: Suggest making the form fields a different colour so they stand out more.
options.explain: Cosmetic. *In the way* is about user-friction, not visual polish. The 7-step flow has structural problems your colour change doesn't touch.

options.label: Recommend collapsing 7 steps to 1 long-scroll page.
options.explain: You replaced one bad pattern with another. Long-scroll KYC forms intimidate; 7 small steps with progress feel achievable. The right move is to remove *unnecessary* steps, not to mash them all together.

options.label: Look at the analytics from the staging cohort — where are users actually dropping off?
options.explain: **Brilliant if data exists.** Real drop-off > opinion drop-off. Vikram pulls the staging numbers; step 6 (the 47-option dropdown) loses 31% of users. Now you have your single biggest target with zero debate.

stages.prompt: **Screen 3**: a beautifully animated transaction-history page Vikram has spent two weekends on. It's polished. It's also the last screen in your critique. Apply question 3: ***"What is the smallest change that helps?"*** With launch in 13 days, what do you decide?

options.label: Ship it as-is. It's polished, it works, and the smallest helpful change before launch is *no change* — protect the launch window for the KYC fixes that actually matter.
options.explain: **This is the senior move.** Critique is not an excuse to redesign everything you see. You correctly identified that the transaction history is *already in the launch-acceptable zone*, and protected scarce engineering hours for the KYC step-6 fix that will actually move retention. Vikram exhales for the first time today.

options.label: Suggest five small polish items — different easing curve, different empty state, different timestamp format.
options.explain: You added 3 days of work to a 13-day runway, on a screen that wasn't broken. The KYC fix won't ship in time because you spent the budget here. You optimised the wrong screen.

options.label: Recommend a full rebuild — the animation library is heavy and slows the app.
options.explain: Two weeks before launch is *not* the time to rebuild. If the perf issue is real, log it post-launch with a measurement. Pre-launch critique should bias toward *smallest helpful change*, not *most thorough one*.

options.label: Cut the transaction-history animation entirely — too risky on low-end Android devices.
options.explain: Possibly true but you have no data to back it. *Cutting* the polish work without measurement is the inverse of the over-polish trap; you traded one untested decision for another. Test on a low-end device first; cut only if measured.

outcomes.perfect: Wednesday's 90-minute critique cut the Refer-a-Friend screen, fixed the KYC step-6 dropdown (3 to 12 grouped options), and protected the transaction-history animation. Saral Pay launches on time. Step-6 retention goes from 69% to 91% in week one. Vikram texts you three weeks later: *"That call saved the launch."* **Diya forwards your message to her own clients as a teaching example.**
outcomes.good: You ran the critique loop but spent budget on the wrong screen, or didn't push back hard enough on a feature that should have been cut. Launch goes okay but with one redesign in the first month. Re-read the lesson on **the smallest change that helps** as the actual hardest of the three questions.
outcomes.learn: You either let *just ship* win, or you ran the critique and turned it into a redesign. Re-read the lesson — especially the section on **critique as triage, not perfection**, and the part about **how protecting the launch is itself a design decision**.

blocks.caption: Try (~60s) · Critique template — Fill 3 boxes: what works, what doesn't, one specific change.

points: Critique is the second design step, not the last. Invite it while changes are cheap.
The 3-question critique: what's the primary action, what breaks with no context, what would a cold reviewer push back on. In that order, every time.
If three reviewers give three different answers to 'what's the primary action', you have a hierarchy problem, not a critique problem.
The spec-first PR: three paragraphs of intent (what changed, why, what we're not doing) above the diff. Free, high-leverage, ritual.
End every critique with decisions in three buckets: fix now, fix later, document and ship. 'Discuss further' is procrastination.

blocks.prompt: Pick a recent design decision from your team. Walk through the 3-question critique on it now: what was the primary action, what would have broken with no context, what would a cold reviewer push back on? What did you miss the first time? Write down the rule you'd add to your team's critique format because of it.

assessment.title: UI/UX Design Foundations — Final Assessment
assessment.description: Seventeen scenario-based questions. Every wrong answer is the kind of thing a smart-but-untrained engineer or PM would actually pick. Pick the answer a senior designer would defend on a Monday standup, not the one that sounds nicest.

choices.label: Top-left, because users always start there
choices.explanation: The top-left rule comes from blank-page reading studies, not from interfaces with active visual elements.

choices.label: On the green Save button at top-right, because contrast outranks position
choices.explanation: Contrast with surroundings beats reading-order priors. The eye is a lazy heuristic engine; it follows the loudest signal.

choices.label: Bottom-left, because that is where the action button is
choices.explanation: Position alone is not a strong enough cue when contrast disagrees. A grey button on a grey screen is camouflage.

choices.label: Wherever the cursor was last hovering
choices.explanation: The cursor's last position influences the second saccade, not the first one.

questions.stem: A teammate says 'the eye naturally goes to the top-left.' On a left-to-right SaaS dashboard with a green Save button at top-right and a grey Save button at bottom-left, where does the eye actually land first?

choices.label: Increase contrast between the element and its background
choices.explanation: Contrast is the cheapest hierarchy. A dark button on a pale card outranks a 24px headline next to it.

choices.label: Add a coloured drop-shadow
choices.explanation: Shadows add depth, not hierarchy. Two shadowed elements still compete for the same attention slot.

choices.label: Surround the element with white space
choices.explanation: Isolation is hierarchy. Anything with breathing room reads as the answer; anything in a crowd reads as a footnote.

choices.label: Bold every label in the form
choices.explanation: If everything is bold, nothing is bold. You have just reset the hierarchy at a higher weight.

questions.stem: Which of these are reliable ways to create primary visual hierarchy without using bigger fonts? (pick two)

choices.label: Because 8 is divisible by 2 and 4, so half-steps and quarter-steps stay on integers across density modes
choices.explanation: 8 has clean factors. A 4px half-step still lands on a pixel; a 7px grid gives you 3.5px half-steps and blurry rendering.

choices.label: Because Apple and Google said so
choices.explanation: Cargo-culting Material guidelines is not a defence. The reason both teams picked 8 is the divisibility, not the brand.

choices.label: Because most screens are 800px or 1600px wide
choices.explanation: Screen width does not interact with the spacing scale in any meaningful way.

choices.label: Because 8 is what Tailwind defaults to
choices.explanation: Tailwind defaults to 4px steps that compose into 8s. Even Tailwind's reason is the divisibility.

questions.stem: Your engineer pushes back: 'Why an 8-point grid? Why not 7 or 10?' Which answer would you defend in code review?

choices.label: It feels claustrophobic and the sections blur together
choices.explanation: Without varied spacing the eye cannot tell what is grouped with what. Identical spacing kills hierarchy.

choices.label: It loads too slowly
choices.explanation: Spacing has nothing to do with load time.

choices.label: The colour palette is wrong
choices.explanation: Colour might be a separate problem; the spacing-only symptom here is the grouping confusion.

choices.label: The buttons are not bold enough
choices.explanation: Buttons can be loud, but if everything around them is the same density, the loudness still feels chaotic.

questions.stem: You inherit a settings page where every input has the same 12px padding, every section has 12px between fields, and every section is 12px from the next section. What is the most likely complaint from users?

choices.label: A 1.25 ratio (major third) keeps headings distinguishable without shouting
choices.explanation: 1.25 to 1.333 are workable for dense interfaces. 1.5 (perfect fifth) is for marketing pages where scale is a feature.

choices.label: You should ship at least seven distinct font sizes so designers have flexibility
choices.explanation: Five is plenty. Seven sizes invites fights about which is the 'right' H3 and produces visual noise.

choices.label: Body text below 14px on web is hostile to users over 35
choices.explanation: 16px body, 14px secondary is a defensible floor. 12px is for badges and timestamps, not paragraphs.

choices.label: Always use two different font families for visual interest
choices.explanation: Two families is for editorial design. SaaS apps rarely need more than one well-chosen family.

questions.stem: Which of these is true about a good type scale on a SaaS app? (pick two)

choices.label: Because hex codes are technical debt; the moment you ship two shades of #3B82F6, you have committed to a manual rename later
choices.explanation: Tokens like primary-500 abstract the meaning from the value. You can swap the brand colour in one line; you cannot grep your way out of #3B82F6 vs #3D80F4 in 200 components.

choices.label: Because hex codes are slower to render than named colours
choices.explanation: There is no rendering cost difference. The cost is human.

choices.label: Because designers prefer HSL
choices.explanation: HSL is useful for picking, but the actual win is naming, not the format.

choices.label: Because hex codes do not work in dark mode
choices.explanation: Hex codes work fine; what fails is the assumption that one shade of grey covers both modes.

questions.stem: Why should you stop pasting hex codes directly into your Tailwind config?

choices.label: Add a loading spinner and disable the button until the request resolves
choices.explanation: Every click is a question; the user is asking 'did it hear me?' A state change inside 100ms is the answer.

choices.label: Show a confirmation modal before sending
choices.explanation: Adds a click. Solves a different problem (intent confirmation), not the unresponsive feeling.

choices.label: Speed up the backend to under 200ms
choices.explanation: Worth doing eventually, but the perceived-responsiveness problem is solved in the UI in five minutes; the backend fix is a sprint.

choices.label: Add a toast that says 'Sent!' on success
choices.explanation: Useful for the success state, but the silent 1.4 seconds is the bug. The toast comes after.

questions.stem: A user clicks 'Send invoice' and the button does nothing visible for 1.4 seconds. The most surgical fix is:

choices.label: Replace 'An error occurred' with 'We could not save your invoice; your card was declined'
choices.explanation: Good microcopy names the cause and points at the next step. Generic errors train learned helplessness.

choices.label: Use 'Submit' on every form button so users learn the pattern
choices.explanation: Buttons should describe the verb the user is doing — 'Save invoice', 'Send link', 'Confirm payment'. 'Submit' is institutional.

choices.label: In an empty state, show what the user would see when full and how to get there
choices.explanation: Empty states are the best onboarding moment in your app. Wasting them on a sad cloud illustration is criminal.

choices.label: Capitalise every noun in CTAs to look more formal
choices.explanation: Title-case CTAs feel like 1990s government forms. Sentence case is friendlier and easier to scan.

questions.stem: Which of these are good microcopy practices? (pick two)

choices.label: Ask: which goal does the colour fail — accessibility, hierarchy, brand, or emotion?
choices.explanation: Critique without a goal is taste. Naming which goal is at risk turns the conversation into something you can act on.

choices.label: Defend the colour by quoting the brand guidelines
choices.explanation: Defensive moves end critique loops; they do not improve them.

choices.label: Change the colour and move on
choices.explanation: If you change without learning why, you will get the same critique on the next screen.

choices.label: Open a Figma comment thread to async the discussion
choices.explanation: Async is fine, but it does not change the quality of the critique. The redirect to a goal is what matters.

questions.stem: Your design lead opens a critique with 'I don't like the colour.' What is the most useful redirect?

choices.label: Write the user-facing change in plain English at the top of the PR description, then the implementation
choices.explanation: Reviewers can then critique the intent before the code. Saves rebase cycles when the intent is wrong.

choices.label: Write the spec doc only after the PR is merged
choices.explanation: That is documentation, not specification. Specs guide; docs record.

choices.label: Always attach a Figma link and skip the prose
choices.explanation: Figma shows what; prose shows why. PRs need the why.

choices.label: Write the migration before the feature
choices.explanation: Useful for DB work; not the spec-first move described in the lesson.

questions.stem: What is the spec-first PR move?

choices.label: About 86px
choices.explanation: 1280 minus 11 gutters of 24px (264) leaves 1016 across 12 columns, giving ~84-86px each. The exact number matters less than knowing how to do the math.

choices.label: About 107px
choices.explanation: That ignores gutters entirely. 1280 / 12 = 107 only if you forget the spaces between columns.

choices.label: About 64px
choices.explanation: Too narrow; you have over-counted gutters.

choices.label: It does not matter; the grid auto-fits
choices.explanation: Auto-fit hides the math but does not eliminate it. A designer who cannot derive column width has no way to spec a card layout.

questions.stem: A 12-column grid with 24px gutters on a 1280px-wide canvas. Roughly what column width does each column get?

choices.label: Semantic colour names like 'bg-surface' and 'text-muted'
choices.explanation: Semantic tokens decouple meaning from value. You can swap the value in dark mode without touching components.

choices.label: Spacing scale with named steps (4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48)
choices.explanation: Named spacing keeps the team off arbitrary 17px paddings. The constraint is the feature.

choices.label: A list of every screen the brand has ever shipped
choices.explanation: That is an inventory, not a token system.

choices.label: All marketing illustrations in SVG
choices.explanation: Useful for a design system, not a token system. Tokens are atomic values.

questions.stem: Which two of these belong in a basic design-token system?

choices.label: When the user must complete or explicitly dismiss a single decision before continuing
choices.explanation: Modals trade context for focus; you should only spend that trade when the decision is genuinely blocking.

choices.label: Whenever you want to draw attention to something new
choices.explanation: That is what banners and inline highlights are for. Modals interrupt; interruptions are expensive.

choices.label: For multi-step settings flows
choices.explanation: Multi-step belongs in a side-sheet or full-screen flow; modals trap state and prevent reference back.

choices.label: Never — modals are always wrong
choices.explanation: Overcorrection. Modals are the right tool for blocking decisions; they are the wrong tool for everything else.

questions.stem: When is a modal the right pattern?

choices.label: Pure RGB primaries fail accessibility on contrast and look like a 1998 status page; semantic tokens with darker, desaturated values are the fix
choices.explanation: Pure red on white is harsh and often fails WCAG AA on small text. Use a semantic token like 'feedback-error' bound to a darker, desaturated red.

choices.label: Red, green, and yellow are culturally inappropriate in India
choices.explanation: They are culturally fine; the objection is craft, not culture.

choices.label: Browsers render pure RGB primaries slower
choices.explanation: There is no rendering penalty; the objection is visual quality and accessibility.

choices.label: There is no objection — these are the standard error colours
choices.explanation: They were the standard in 2005. Modern systems use desaturated values for the same reason.

questions.stem: A mid-size Bengaluru SaaS ships a settings screen that uses #FF0000 for error, #00FF00 for success, and #FFFF00 for warning. What is the senior-design objection?

choices.label: Users do not read screens; they scan for the loudest, most isolated, most differently-coloured element first
choices.explanation: The visual system optimises for energy. It picks shortcuts; your job is to make the shortcuts lead to the right place.

choices.label: Users have lower IQ than designers think
choices.explanation: Has nothing to do with IQ. The same shortcuts apply to the designer's own eye.

choices.label: Users always click the first button they see
choices.explanation: Often, but not always. The 'first button' is whatever wins the contrast war, which may not be top-left.

choices.label: Animations distract users from the main content
choices.explanation: Animations can compete for attention, but the lazy-heuristic point applies to static screens too.

questions.stem: What does 'the eye is a lazy heuristic engine' mean in practice?

choices.label: What is this screen's single most important action, and how do I know?
choices.explanation: If three people answer differently, the hierarchy is broken. This is the cheapest critique question in the world.

choices.label: What would break if the user opened this with no context?
choices.explanation: Edge cases hide in the assumed context. Asking the cold-open question surfaces them.

choices.label: Is this on-brand?
choices.explanation: Brand is a useful filter, not a critique question. It rarely surfaces structural problems.

choices.label: Did the engineer follow the spec?
choices.explanation: Process question, not a design question. Belongs in a different review.

questions.stem: You are running a design critique. Which two questions are most likely to surface a real problem?

choices.label: Ask which job the button should pop for — primary action, edge case, or compliance — and design the contrast accordingly
choices.explanation: 'Pop' is a symptom request. Naming the job converts it into a hierarchy decision you can defend.

choices.label: Move the button. Customer is always right.
choices.explanation: PMs are not customers, and 'pop' is not a spec. Moving without asking why guarantees a follow-up move next sprint.

choices.label: Refuse and say 'design owns the layout'
choices.explanation: Tribal moves kill cross-functional trust. Better to translate the request into a clear question.

choices.label: Add a red border
choices.explanation: Adds noise without adding hierarchy. The screen now has two loud things instead of one.

questions.stem: A PM at your Pune-based SaaS asks 'can we just move the button to make it pop?' What is the senior-design response?

project.title: Capstone: Rescue the 11pm onboarding screen
project.prompt:
## The ask

It is 11pm on a Friday. Your co-founder, who runs a 25-person Bengaluru SaaS that sells expense-management to small businesses, slacks you a screenshot of their current onboarding screen. There are 14 form fields, three of which are optional, and a grey 'Submit' button at the bottom-left. The activation rate is 38%. He says: *'bro design this properly na, kuch toh kar.'*

You have until Sunday night.

## Deliverables

1. **A redesigned onboarding flow** in your tool of choice (Figma, Excalidraw, or even hand-drawn and photographed). Cover at minimum:
   - the welcome / first-screen state
   - the data-entry steps (you may split the 14 fields across multiple screens or remove some — defend your choices)
   - the success state
   - one error state
2. **A short written defence (300-500 words)** that names:
   - the visual hierarchy you chose, and why
   - the grid and spacing scale you used
   - the type and color tokens you defined (even just five values is fine)
   - one interaction or microcopy change you made and the user behaviour it should change
3. **A self-critique using the 3-question critique** from Lesson 5: what is the single most important action, what breaks with no context, and what would a cold reviewer push back on.

## Submission rules

- Be specific. 'A friendly colour palette' is not a defence. 'A primary blue (#1F6FEB) bound to `interaction-default`, used only on the single primary action per screen, with a desaturated neutral surface to keep the form quiet' is.
- Name your tradeoffs. If you cut three fields, say which three and what you assume happens to the data.
- Keep India-anchored. Your user is a 35-year-old accountant at a 12-person firm in Indore who has used Tally for fifteen years and Excel for twenty.

credential.title: UI/UX Design Foundations
credential.description: Holder can design a small SaaS interface from the ground up — set a grid, build a token system, direct the eye through visual hierarchy, write microcopy that carries weight, and run a critique loop on their own work without flinching.
